items.title: Budget 2027 : prendre le temps de bien faire n’est pas perdre du temps
items.description: Dans une publication partagée sur les réseaux sociaux attribuée à un média, les auteurs insinuent que le projet de loi de finances 2027 n’a pas encore été transmis à l’Assemblée nationale, alors que l’article 124 de la Constitution en fixe le dépôt au 15 octobre. Le constat de date est exact, et le Gouvernement ne l’esquive pas. Mais réduire la préparation du budget 2027 à un « retard », c’est passer à côté de l’essentiel : la Guinée est en train de changer, en une seule année, la manière dont elle construit, vote et exécute son budget. Ce changement exige de la rigueur, et la rigueur exige du temps. Le cap est fixé. Les conférences budgétaires se sont achevées le vendredi 20 novembre, après cinq jours d’échanges avec les ministères et institutions. Les derniers arbitrages sont engagés, et le projet de loi de finances 2027 sera transmis à l’Assemblée nationale avant le 30 novembre. L’objectif est clair : sous réserve de la procédure parlementaire, une loi de finances adoptée et promulguée au plus tard le 31 décembre 2026. Ce qui compte pour les Guinéens, ce n’est pas la date de dépôt, c’est d’avoir un budget en vigueur au 1er janvier. Ce sera le cas, et ce sera le retour à un calendrier budgétaire régulier. Ce calendrier répond à trois exigences que l’article passe sous silence : une transition budgétaire sans précédent, le retour à la normale après une année 2026 décalée, et une mobilisation renforcée des recettes publiques. Une année budgétaire 2026 hors normes, qu’il fallait d’abord stabiliser Rappelons les faits. En raison des circonstances exceptionnelles liées au calendrier électoral, la loi de finances initiale 2026 n’a été promulguée que le 31 mars 2026. Le budget de l’année en cours a donc été exécuté sur neuf mois au lieu de douze. Il fallait ensuite le corriger. La loi de finances rectificative 2026 a été adoptée par l’Assemblée nationale le 31 octobre pour son volet recettes, puis le 7 novembre pour son volet dépenses. Elle porte les recettes à 60 064 milliards GNF et les dépenses à 67 925,87 milliards GNF, et ramène le déficit à 2,01 % du PIB contre 2,07 % prévus initialement. Aucun gestionnaire sérieux ne bâtit le budget de l’année suivante sur des chiffres dont il sait qu’ils vont changer. Le budget 2027 ne pouvait être solidement cadré qu’une fois la base 2026 arrêtée par la représentation nationale. Déposer à la mi-octobre un texte fondé sur des hypothèses aussitôt dépassées aurait respecté la lettre du calendrier, mais pas son esprit : offrir aux députés un budget sincère. Une réforme historique : le passage au budget-programme dès le 1er janvier 2027 Ce que l’article qualifie de « pleine préparation » est en réalité un basculement que la Guinée attend depuis des années. À partir de 2027, tous les ministères passeront du budget de moyens au budget-programme. L’État ne votera plus seulement des lignes de dépenses, mais des politiques publiques assorties d’objectifs et d’indicateurs de résultats. Ce chantier a été lancé au plus haut niveau. Le Premier ministre a présidé lui-même, le 24 septembre 2026, les Journées d’échanges sur la réforme du budget-programme. Du 16 au 20 novembre, 37 ministères et institutions ont défendu leurs avant-projets lors des conférences budgétaires, après une revue des cadres de dépenses à moyen terme (CDMT) de chaque département. Une telle refonte ne se fait pas en recopiant les tableaux de l’année précédente. Chaque ministère doit redéfinir ses programmes, ses actions et ses indicateurs. Le temps consacré à ce travail n’est pas un temps perdu : c’est ce qui permettra, dès 2027, de savoir ce que produit chaque franc guinéen dépensé. Comme l’a résumé le Secrétaire général du ministère de l’Économie, des Finances et du Budget : « Ce que nous finançons, nous devons pouvoir en mesurer les résultats. » Aucun risque pour la continuité de l’État Il faut enfin rassurer les citoyens, les agents publics et les partenaires : ce décalage ne met en péril ni le paiement des salaires, ni le fonctionnement des services publics, ni les engagements de l’État. Le cadre organique des finances publiques prévoit les mécanismes garantissant la continuité budgétaire, et le Gouvernement s’engage à ce que la représentation nationale dispose du temps nécessaire pour examiner pleinement le texte. Le dépôt tardif ne retire en rien aux députés leur droit d’examen. Le Gouvernement assume son choix : celui d’un budget sincère plutôt que précipité, construit sur une base 2026 consolidée, structuré en programmes mesurables, aligné sur Simandou 2040 et nourri des recommandations du Parlement. Les travaux techniques se poursuivent entre les ministères et les services des Finances pour les derniers ajustements, avant l’examen en Conseil interministériel puis en Conseil des ministres. Le calendrier est désormais arrêté : transmission du projet de loi de finances 2027 à l’Assemblée nationale avant le 30 novembre, pour une promulgation visée au plus tard le 31 décembre 2026, sous réserve de la procédure parlementaire. La Guinée ouvrira 2027 avec un budget opérationnel, une nouvelle architecture de gestion publique et des priorités de financement clairement établies. Le retard se mesure en semaines. Les bénéfices d’un budget enfin orienté vers les résultats se mesureront en années. Service d’Information du Gouvernement L’article Budget 2027 : prendre le temps de bien faire n’est pas perdre du temps est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Navy intercepts 89,000 litres of stolen crude, illegal diesel in Rivers
items.description: By Kingsley Omonobi The Nigerian Navy has intercepted about 35,000 litres of suspected stolen crude oil and uncovered an illegal refining site containing an additional 54,000 litres of suspected illegally refined Automotive Gas Oil (AGO) in Rivers State. The operation, conducted on November 22 by personnel of Nigerian Navy Ship (NNS) Pathfinder around Okarki Creek and Okarki Community in Ahoada West Local Government Area, followed credible intelligence. In a statement on Monday, the Director of Naval Information, Navy Captain Abiodun Folorunsho, said the naval personnel intercepted a wooden boat conveying about 150 sacks containing suspected stolen crude oil. He said a subsequent operation in the adjoining area led to the discovery of an illegal refining site containing approximately 10 dugout pits, 180 sacks and a storage container holding an estimated 54,000 litres of suspected illegally refined AGO. According to him, the combined volume of petroleum products recovered or identified during the operation was approximately 89,000 litres. “The boat, its contents and the refining site, including the stored products, were handled in accordance with established anti-crude oil theft procedures,” the statement said. The Navy described the operation as part of its sustained campaign to disrupt the supply networks supporting crude oil theft and illegal refining activities in the Niger Delta. It said intercepting the suspected stolen crude oil and dismantling associated refining infrastructure would help deny oil thieves access to petroleum resources while addressing environmental degradation and revenue losses. The Service reaffirmed its commitment to intelligence-driven operations to protect critical oil and gas infrastructure, support national crude oil production and safeguard Nigeria’s economic interests. It added that operations would continue across the Niger Delta creeks to combat crude oil theft and illegal refining. items.title: NEC approves additional N130bn for rehabilitation of police colleges
items.description: The National Economic Council (NEC) has approved an additional N130 billion for the ongoing rehabilitation of police training institutions across the country. The council also endorsed two major development projects involving proposed World Bank financing of 850 million dollars. The projects are aimed at strengthening disaster preparedness, climate resilience and early childhood development across the country. Gov. Peter Mbah of Enugu, Chairman of the NEC Ad-Hoc Committee on Rehabilitation of Police Training Institutions, disclosed this while briefing newsmen. Mbah briefed newsmen on the outcome of the 162nd NEC meeting, held virtually and chaired by Vice-President Kashim Shettima. NAN recalls that NEC, on Dec. 3, 2025, approved N100 billion for rehabilitating training institutions for the police and other security agencies. The additional N130 billion brings the total approved funding to N230 billion. Mbah disclosed that rehabilitation work was ongoing at 13 locations nationwide, with about 30 per cent of the work completed. He explained that the additional N130 billion would accelerate the rehabilitation, upgrade training facilities and strengthen the capacity of police institutions. According to him, the intervention would enable the institutions to accommodate increased recruitment and training requirements. The governor said the intervention would also support preparations for recruiting 50,000 police personnel. “It will also improve the country’s security training infrastructure,” Mbah said. On the economy, the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Mr Taiwo Oyedele, informed the council that Nigeria’s economic indicators had continued to improve. He said the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew by 4.43 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, compared with 4.23 per cent in the corresponding period of 2025. He disclosed that headline inflation declined for the fifth consecutive month to 14.06 per cent in October 2026, its lowest level since September 2020. “External reserves stood at 54.87 billion dollars as of November 12, 2026,” he said. The minister said Nigeria’s trade surplus increased from N10.2 trillion in the first half of 2025 to N20.1 trillion in the corresponding period of 2026. “Net revenue distributed through the Federation Account Allocation Committee rose by 44 per cent, from N15.2 trillion in 2024 to N21.9 trillion in 2025,” he said. Oyedele, however, observed that the improving economic indicators had yet to translate sufficiently into relief for households and businesses. “This is particularly in the areas of food prices, electricity costs, access to affordable credit and employment,” he said. He noted that food inflation remained elevated at 19.13 per cent in October, while high lending rates and energy costs continued to pressure businesses and household incomes. Meanwhile, the council approved two memoranda presented through the Federal Ministry of Budget and Economic Planning, headed by Sen. Atiku Bagudu. Bagudu explained that the first concerned the proposed 350 million dollars Accelerating Resilience through Investment Systems and Engagement (ARISE-Nigeria) Project. He said the six-year, World Bank-supported programme was designed to strengthen Nigeria’s capacity to anticipate, prepare for and respond to floods, droughts, fires and other natural disasters. The minister said the programme would improve emergency operations centres, early warning systems, weather monitoring and disaster response financing at federal and state levels. “Between five and 10 states are expected to participate in the initial phase. “Selection will be based on disaster risk exposure, institutional readiness and commitment to emergency preparedness,” he said. The minister said the second memorandum concerned Nigeria’s State-Led Early Childhood Development Programme. “It is designed to improve children’s access to healthcare, nutrition, early learning and protection services across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory,” he said. Bagudu said the initiative was expected to receive support through a proposed 500 million dollars World Bank financing arrangement. He added that the Global Financing Facility had indicated potential additional grant support of 30 million dollars. “Under the programme, early childhood development hubs will connect primary healthcare facilities with childcare, preschool education and other essential social services. “This will particularly benefit underserved communities,” he said. Bagudu said state governors were expected to provide leadership in implementation, resource mobilisation and accountability. On the National Identity Management Commission (NIMC) Act, 2026, Gov. Sheriff Oborevwori of Delta said the council called for stronger collaboration between the commission and state governments. Oborevwori said the collaboration would accelerate the registration of Nigerians and improve the integration of the National Identification Number into public services. He urged state governments to fast-track identity registration and data capture to ensure that all Nigerians were covered by the national identity system. On pension reforms, Gov. Abdullahi Sule of Nasarawa said the council urged state governors to formally adopt implementation timelines for the Contributory Pension Scheme. He said governors were also advised to direct their administrative and finance teams to work with the National Pension Commission (PenCom) on the necessary arrangements The post NEC approves additional N130bn for rehabilitation of police colleges appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Foreigners taking over Ghana’s retail market a worrying trend – Kumasi Mayor
items.description: Kumasi Mayor Richard Ofori-Agyemang Boadi has described the growing involvement of foreign nationals in Ghana’s retail trade as a worrying trend, warning that it could undermine the interests of local businesses if urgent action is not taken. He says the situation requires careful intervention within the confines of the law to protect Ghanaian traders without damaging the country’s international relations. Speaking on JoyNews’ The Pulse on Monday, November 23, the Mayor said he was working with the Ghana Investment Promotion Centre (GIPC) and the Ashanti Regional Coordinating Council to identify appropriate measures to address the issue. “The new phenomenon that is happening within the Greater Kumasi enclave, where foreigners seem to have taken over our retail market, is a worrying trend, and we are looking for the best way to handle it, in order not to let Ghana get negative ramifications internationally,” he said. His comments follow growing tension at the Suame industrial enclave in the Ashanti Region, where local artisans reportedly attacked some foreign spare-parts dealers over allegations of unfair competition and pricing. The incident has reignited concerns over the presence of foreign nationals in retail businesses at Suame Magazine in Kumasi. The Mayor also blamed some Ghanaian business owners for contributing to the situation by renting out their shops to foreign nationals. He argued that the premises were privately owned and that some Ghanaian spare parts dealers were allowing foreign traders to operate from their shops. “Those shops there are not owned by government. They are owned by Ghanaians, some of whom even spare parts dealers, and they let out these shops to the so-called foreign nationals,” he said. Mr Boadi called for urgent action to protect Ghanaian business interests, warning that continued foreign dominance of the retail market could leave local traders struggling in the coming years. “If we don’t do something about it and the trend goes on in five, 10 years, I’m telling you Ghanaian businessmen are going to become poor,” he cautioned. He said any intervention must be guided by the law, as authorities continue engagements with the relevant institutions to find a way forward.

items.title: Cause of fire at Northern Regional Coordinating Council yet to be established – GNFS
items.description: The Ghana National Fire Service (GNFS) says investigations are underway to establish the cause of a fire that destroyed parts of the Northern Regional Coordinating Council building in Tamale. The fire, which affected three offices, started in the office of the Northern Regional Minister’s secretary before spreading to the office of the Coordinating Chief Director and part of the Minister’s office. Speaking on JoyNews’ The Pulse on Monday, the Northern Regional Officer of the GNFS, Hudu Baba, said the Service was yet to conclude, as investigators were conducting further assessments. He explained that the building houses a key government institution in the region, requiring a thorough investigation to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident. “Our investigating team are currently working at it to reveal the cause,” he said. Several documents and computers were reportedly destroyed in the fire, while the full extent of the damage is yet to be assessed. The Northern Regional Officer of the GNFS said the Service received a distress call at about 4:00 a.m. on Monday. He said firefighters from the Tamale Hospital Fire Station initially responded to the incident but had to call for reinforcement from the regional headquarters substation and the Tamale Central Fire Station. The three fire crews worked together to bring the blaze under control before extinguishing it at 5:45 a.m. Mr Baba said firefighters managed to prevent the fire from spreading through the entire office space of the Northern Regional Minister and other sections of the building. “Had it not been that, I think the entire office would have burnt, including the other side of the facility, which is the upper fifth floor of the entire Regional Coordinating Council,” he said.

items.title: Batteries au lithium : l’Algérie lance une usine de 5 GWh sous le pilotage de Karim Zaghib
items.description: L'Algérie lance officiellement un projet de réalisation d’une usine de batteries au lithium. Le projet est confié par le président de la République, Abdelmadjid Tebboune, au spécialiste algérien installé au Canada, Karim Zaghib . Le projet a fait l’objet d’une réunion de travail présidée ce lundi 23 novembre par le chef de l’État, en présence de plusieurs ministres. Selon un communiqué de la présidence de la République, le président Tebboune a nommé à cette occasion le professeur Karim Zaghib à la tête du projet. Zaghib est chargé « d'étudier et de suivre les différentes étapes de réalisation techniques et technologiques, sous la supervision du maître d'ouvrage qui est le ministère de l'Énergie et des Énergies renouvelables, par l'intermédiaire de la société Sonelgaz International », lit-on dans le communiqué. Karim Zaghib : un projet « ambitieux » et d’une « grande crédibilité » Il s'agit d’un projet « ambitieux et d’une grande importance dans le domaine des batteries », a indiqué le professeur Zaghib à sa sortie du bureau du président. La réalisation d’une usine de batteries en Algérie est un projet d’une « grande crédibilité », a assuré le spécialiste, d'autant plus, a-t-il ajouté, que le pays « est doté d’un écosystème intégré et exceptionnel et dispose des métaux critiques ». « L'Algérie fabriquera des batteries au lithium pour le marché national et pour le monde, et nous les utiliserons également pour le stockage de l'énergie », a-t-il déclaré à l’issue de la réunion. L’objectif, selon Karim Zaghib, est d'augmenter la production de fer et de phosphate à transformer en cathodes pour batteries au lithium-ion. L'usine envisagée aura une capacité de 5 gigawattheures, avec une utilisation qui ne se limitera pas seulement aux voitures électriques, mais qui s'étendra aussi au stockage de l’énergie, a-t-il révélé. « Il faut réfléchir aux perspectives de ces projets, qui sont des projets prometteurs pour l’Algérie, pour couvrir les besoins intérieurs et aller aussi à l'export vers les marchés africain, européen, nord-américain et asiatique, comme la Chine », a déclaré le chef du projet. Karim Zaghib, l’un des plus grands spécialistes mondiaux de la batterie au lithium Karim Zaghib est membre du Haut Conseil scientifique de la communauté algérienne établie à l’étranger, créé récemment à l’initiative du président de la République. Né à Constantine en 1963, il s’est installé depuis 1995 au Québec où il est considéré comme l’un des meilleurs spécialistes mondiaux de la batterie au lithium. Il détient plus de 600 brevets et 60 licences. En 2015, son nom a été cité dans la liste des scientifiques les plus influents du monde établie par la société Clarivate Analytics, spécialisée dans l’analyse de la production scientifique. L’article Batteries au lithium : l’Algérie lance une usine de 5 GWh sous le pilotage de Karim Zaghib est apparu en premier sur TSA .

Electoral Act not responsible for rising campaign violence — Adegbonmire
items.description: By Cynthia Alo & Kafayat Kokumo Chairman of the Senate Ad Hoc Committee on Electoral Reforms, Adeniyi Adegbonmire, has said the Electoral Act is not responsible for rising cases of campaign violence across the country, insisting that the problem lies in the failure of relevant institutions to enforce its provisions. Adegbonmire, who is also the Chairman of the Senate Committee on Judiciary, Human Rights, and Legal Matters, said the National Assembly had made adequate provisions for electoral offences in the Electoral Act and empowered the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to prosecute offenders. Speaking during an interview on Arise Television on Monday , he said the responsibility for addressing electoral violence rested on INEC, the police and other security agencies, which must ensure strict enforcement of the law. He said: “The National Assembly passed an Electoral Act, the intention being to set out everything that relates to electoral matters, and in that Electoral Act there are electoral offences and it gives INEC the powers to prosecute. “So, for me, when it comes to the Act itself, it’s made provisions for what you refer to, and so when it comes to all of these reports that we hear, electoral skirmishes here and there, I don’t think it’s a function of the Act. It’s a function of how to ensure whoever, INEC, police, security agents take advantage of the provisions of the Act.” The senator also faulted what he described as inconsistent media reports on political violence, urging journalists to condemn attacks regardless of the political party involved or the identity of those responsible. According to him, describing attacks against the ruling party as public protests while reporting similar incidents involving opposition parties as attacks by thugs could encourage a biased perception of political violence. He said: “It is the collective responsibility of all of us to ensure that acts of violence in whatever form or fashion are condemned regardless of who is the victim or who are the perpetrators.” On the Senate’s recent call for investigations into reported campaign violence, Adegbonmire clarified that the resolution was not an indictment of security agencies but an effort to draw attention to the growing threat and urge relevant institutions to act. He disclosed that security agencies were investigating some incidents but cautioned against making arrests without proper investigations, noting that not everyone present at a violent rally necessarily participated in the violence. “If we are going to follow the law, let’s follow it strictly regardless of what advantage or disadvantage it may visit upon us. Let everybody follow the rule of law,” he said. On concerns about voter safety ahead of the 2027 general elections, the senator expressed confidence in the ability of security agencies to protect voters. He cited the governorship elections in Anambra and Osun states, where Governors Chukwuma Soludo and Ademola Adeleke emerged winners, arguing that the outcomes reflected the choices of the electorate despite pockets of violence. He said there was no empirical basis for predicting that the 2027 elections would not reflect the people’s choice. The senator also defended INEC’s planned nationwide mock accreditation exercise scheduled for November 28, saying the exercise should be seen as an opportunity to identify and correct operational challenges before the presidential and National Assembly elections on January 16, 2027. He said Nigerians should not condemn the commission if technical challenges emerged during the mock exercise, as identifying such problems ahead of the actual polls was its primary purpose. On the proposed deployment of artificial intelligence, AI, in the electoral process, Adegbonmire said the Senate would wait for INEC to publish its guidelines before scrutinising the proposed framework. He said the commission had indicated that it was developing guidelines for the deployment of the technology, adding that lawmakers would examine the document and seek necessary clarifications or corrections once it was released. “I would prefer to wait for INEC to publish their guidelines and then we start to interrogate it if we feel that there’s a need to have certain corrections or clarifications done,” he said. The post Electoral Act not responsible for rising campaign violence — Adegbonmire appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: La souveraineté informationnelle de l’Alliance des États du Sahel soutenue par la Russie : analyse géopolitique de Tafouk TV
items.description: À télécharger Lire la note (PDF) Le 29 octobre 2026, la chaîne sahélienne Tafouk TV a retransmis en direct le signal de la chaîne russe RT en français, couvrant le Sommet Russie-Afrique (28-29 octobre) tenu à Moscou. Créée conjointement par les autorités du Mali, du Burkina Faso et du Niger, la chaîne a reçu le soutien de la Russie à travers la signature d’un accord de coopération avec le média RT en juillet 2026. Si les détails de cet accord n’ont pas été rendus publics, l’analyse des contenus diffusés par la chaîne sahélienne met déjà en évidence un partage de contenu asymétrique du média russe vers Tafouk TV, ainsi que des intérêts éditoriaux communs. Les autorités des trois pays de la Confédération des États du Sahel, ou Alliance des États du Sahel (AES), ont créé des médias conjoints afin d’assurer leur souveraineté informationnelle. Dès lors, dans quelle mesure Tafouk TV est un projet médiatique endogène ? L’article La souveraineté informationnelle de l’Alliance des États du Sahel soutenue par la Russie : analyse géopolitique de Tafouk TV est apparu en premier sur IRIS .

items.title: Instagram removes Polish tourist’s video accusing Daura Emir of sexual assault
items.description: Instagram has removed a video shared by Polish tourist Mirka Cze, in which she accused the Emir of Daura, Faruk Umar Faruk, of grabbing her breast during a visit to his palace in Katsina State. Cze disclosed the removal in a post on her Instagram page on Monday, saying she believed the video was taken down after several users reported it. “It seems that because too many people were clicking on the ‘report’ button, the Instagram algorithm has removed the video. I didn’t,” she wrote. The tourist said she had asked Meta, Instagram’s parent company, to review the decision and restore the video. She added that she was relieved other bloggers had reposted the footage, allowing it to remain in circulation. Cze said she decided to speak publicly about the alleged incident because she had recorded evidence and wanted to draw attention to the experiences of women who might have suffered sexual abuse but had no opportunity to speak out. “When this bad experience happened to me at the palace of the Emir of Daura, I felt I needed to share it. Because it happened to me. Because I had a chance and a tool to record it, and because I believe it happens to so many other women who don’t have a chance to speak up,” she said in the Instagram post. She explained that her visit to the palace had initially been welcoming, with the emir offering her local food while palace guards showed her around the premises, including the stables, where she rode a horse. However, she said she became uncomfortable when she was left alone with the traditional ruler, unlike her previous visits to other palaces where guards were present during her interactions with monarchs. The Polish tourist also said she had visited 18 other locations and palaces across Nigeria without experiencing sexual assault before the alleged incident in Daura. Reflecting on the reactions to her earlier post, Cze said most people had shown her kindness and support, although some questioned her account. She added that she needed time away from the controversy to recover emotionally and move on from the experience. “I’m writing this with tears coming down, and I really feel that for the healing and for getting in better mental space, I need to start thinking about other things and places to leave Nigeria and what happened there behind,” she wrote. “I’ve seen the comments and messages, and would say that 90 per cent were supportive and kind, but I need my space now.” Meta had yet to publicly explain why the video was removed as of Monday. The post Instagram removes Polish tourist’s video accusing Daura Emir of sexual assault appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: L’armée russe a-t-elle assez d’hommes pour continuer la guerre ?
items.description: Selon les estimations du chercheur allemand Janis Kluge, à partir des données budgétaires du ministère des Finances russe, l'armée russe a signé environ 34 000 nouveaux contrats le mois dernier, et 297 000 depuis le début de l'année – contre 335 000 à la même période en 2025, soit une baisse de 11,3 % Russian recruitment in late 2026 », Russianomics, 22 novembre 2026.'> 1 . Ce chiffre, mis en perspective avec les communiqués de l'État-major des forces armées ukrainiennes, qui recensent jour par jour les pertes russes (tués et blessés), indique que Moscou a perdu plus d'hommes qu'elle n'en a recruté en octobre. Il s'agit du sixième mois consécutif où les pertes dépassent les recrutements, et l'écart n'a cessé de se creuser depuis juillet : en octobre, il a atteint environ 20 000 hommes, son plus haut niveau depuis janvier 2025. Le déficit d'hommes dont souffre Moscou doit être lu à la lumière des chiffres compilés par les services statistiques russes, auxquels les groupes de hackers biélorusse Cyber Partisans et ukrainien Silent Crow ont eu accès. Ces données, dont une analyse des médias indépendants Mediazona et Meduza a été publiée aujourd'hui, lundi 23 novembre, montrent en effet que les pertes subies par l'armée russe en Ukraine ont dépassé la barre des 490 000 morts entre février 2022 et fin septembre 2026. Les fichiers, jugés authentiques par Mediazona au terme de deux semaines d'analyse, proviennent de l'agence de statistiques russe Rosstat, et contiennent des enregistrements de décès anonymisés accompagnés de détails tels que le lieu et la cause du décès. Что утечка Росстата говорит о потерях России на войне В начале ноября хакерские группы « Киберпартизаны » и Silent Crow объявили о взломе Росстата. Они получили доступ не только к сайту, но и к внутренним сетям — это терабайты данных, включая данные о смертности, которые не… pic.twitter.com/pC91IRqm0A — Медиазона (@mediazzzona) November 23, 2026 Selon une estimation de Meduza, qui tient compte des décès non encore enregistrés, le nombre total de morts s'élèverait à 700 000 hommes, ce qui suggère des pertes totales d'environ 2 millions de combattants Данные Росстата раскрыли гибель на войне 500 тысяч человек — и эти данные настоящие. С учетом пропавших цифра на сегодня — около 700 тысяч », Mediazona , 23 novembre 2026.'> 2 . Ce dernier chiffre est supérieur au bilan de l'État-major des forces armées ukrainiennes, qui estime qu'environ 1,6 million de combattants russes ont été tués ou blessés depuis février 2022. Il tombe également au-dessus des estimations produites par des chercheurs indépendants, comme celles du CSIS (environ 1,4 million de tués, blessés et disparus à la fin juin) ou de T he Economist (entre 1,1 et 1,5 million en mai). Les données de Rosstat montrent que la guerre est la principale cause de mortalité chez les hommes en âge de travailler à l'échelle du pays depuis 2025. Elles permettent également d'estimer qu'au moins 0,9 % des hommes russes âgés de moins de 60 ans au début de la guerre ont été tués en Ukraine depuis 2022. Rapportées à la population, ces pertes frappent surtout la Sibérie et l'Extrême-Orient : en Transbaïkalie, près d'un habitant sur 80 serait mort à la guerre depuis 2022, soit 18 fois plus qu'à Moscou. L’article L'armée russe a-t-elle assez d'hommes pour continuer la guerre ? est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: Regular JHS pupils must complete three years before BECE – WAEC
items.description: Regular Junior High School (JHS) pupils must complete all three years of the programme before sitting the Basic Education Certificate Examination (BECE), the West African Examinations Council (WAEC) has reiterated. The Council says students enrolled in regular schools are not eligible to register for the private BECE, which is reserved for individuals who are not in regular school and candidates seeking to improve grades obtained in previous examinations. Speaking on JoyNews’ Top Story on Monday, November 23, 2026, WAEC’s Deputy Director of Public Affairs, Lilian Frimpong, said it was illegal for regular JHS students to register for the private examination. “We have stated clearly in the post that it is illegal for a regular candidate in JHS to register for this exam. So it is already and we have posted that. If you’re in a school and you are in JHS, you are not supposed to write the private exams. That means that you are supposed to go through the three years and write as a school candidate,” she said. Frimpong explained that the private BECE caters for first-time candidates who are not enrolled in regular schools, as well as individuals who have previously sat the examination and want to improve their grades. She said first-time private candidates must be at least 13 years old. “The first one is for first-timers. If you’re an individual, you should be one who is not in a regular school. And we have an age limit. You should not be less than 13 years. And it’s also for resitters. Means students who have previously sat for the exams,” she stated. She said the Education Minister’s recent directive was a reaffirmation of existing eligibility requirements rather than the introduction of a new WAEC rule. Frimpong said regular school candidates are expected to complete the three-year JHS programme because their eligibility to write the school examination is tied to continuous assessment requirements. “For us, WAEC, if you haven’t gotten to Form Three and you write the exams, we usually see those candidates and we rate them as unqualified candidates. Because one of our requirements for the school exam is for you to have the three years continuous assessment. So if you skipped, you are unqualified because then you have skipped a basic requirement that we need to be able to grade you,” she said. WAEC’s eligibility rules for school candidates require them to be in the third year of Junior High Schools approved by the Ghana Education Service. The clarification comes amid renewed government efforts to stop students in JHS 1 and JHS 2 from sitting the BECE ahead of schedule. In April 2026, Education Minister Haruna Iddrisu announced plans to restrict the examination to students in JHS 3, arguing that allowing younger students to sit the examination contravened existing GES and WAEC guidelines. The Minister linked early registration to persistently poor BECE results, arguing that some students who write the examination ahead of schedule are inadequately prepared. On November 23, 2026, he announced a two-year ban on pupils in JHS 1 and JHS 2 who attempt to write the BECE before completing the required period. He directed the Director-General of the Ghana Education Service to communicate the directive to regional directors and headteachers for immediate implementation. Government says the measure is intended to promote discipline and improve planning for the number of candidates expected to sit the examination each year. WAEC has urged the public to take note of the eligibility requirements as the government moves to enforce the restrictions.

items.title: UniMAC graduates 1,414 as university targets AI-driven creative economy
items.description: The University of Media, Arts and Communication (UniMAC) has graduated 1,414 students, recording a 57.6 per cent increase over its 2025 graduating class. The graduates received their qualifications at the first session of the university’s fifth congregation, held on Saturday, 21 November 2026. The graduating class represents a significant increase from the 897 students who graduated in 2025, reflecting the expanding reach of an institution whose academic mandate spans journalism, film and television, languages, arts and strategic communication. The ceremony also marked the first congregation presided over by entrepreneur Ernest Ofori Sarpong following his investiture as UniMAC’s first Chancellor a day earlier. Beyond the conferment of degrees, the occasion provided an opportunity for the university’s leadership to outline its ambitions, particularly as artificial intelligence (AI), digital platforms and changing audience behaviour reshape the industries for which its graduates are being trained. Addressing the congregation, Mr Ofori Sarpong said the university had a distinctive responsibility to influence how Ghana creates, communicates, preserves its identity and engages with the wider world. He cautioned that while artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies were transforming information production, storytelling, language translation and creative production, technology alone could not replace human imagination, ethical judgement and cultural understanding. “The question should not simply be how quickly we can adopt AI, but how intelligently, ethically and creatively we can deploy it,” he said. He urged UniMAC to position itself at the forefront of conversations on the future of creativity, the ethical application of artificial intelligence, the preservation of indigenous languages and the contribution of the creative economy to national development. His remarks reflected a wider challenge confronting Ghana’s media and creative industries, where technological advancement is creating new opportunities for content production, distribution and commercialisation while placing fresh demands on the skills and professional standards of practitioners. For the graduates, he said, academic qualifications must be accompanied by integrity, creativity, continuous learning and a commitment to excellence. Vice-Chancellor Professor Eric Opoku Mensah said the changing relationship between media, arts, languages and communication required universities to rethink how they train professionals. He explained that the disciplines were no longer isolated areas of professional practice, as storytellers increasingly needed technological understanding, artists had to appreciate the influence of digital platforms, and communicators needed the capacity to engage multilingual and multicultural audiences. He said UniMAC’s responsibility was not merely to respond to technological change but to prepare students to understand, navigate and contribute to shaping it. Professor Mensah disclosed that the university had developed and launched its first five-year strategic plan, covering 2026 to 2030, to provide a framework for its ambition to become a world-class centre of excellence in communication scholarship, media innovation, language development and the creative economy. The plan identifies academic excellence and curriculum innovation, research and knowledge production, infrastructure development, digital transformation, human resource development, financial sustainability, internationalisation, governance and institutional efficiency, as well as branding and visibility, as its major priorities. He said the plan would require collective commitment from management, staff, students, alumni, industry and development partners to translate its objectives into measurable institutional progress. The university’s academic growth is already reflected in its expanding postgraduate programmes and professional training offerings. According to the Vice-Chancellor, demand for postgraduate education increased by 58 per cent in 2026, following the introduction of programmes including the MSc in Strategic Brand Management and Communication, MA in Sustainability and Environmental Communication, and MPhil top-up in Development Communication. UniMAC currently offers approximately 30 programmes across its constituent institutes, while its Short Courses Coordinating Unit mounted 17 courses during the year, training more than 1,500 participants. Among the short courses offered were AI-Powered Content Creation: Mastering Production, Broadcast and Management, Language Proficiency, Digital Marketing Communication and Office Management (Foreign Language Option). The university also held its inaugural State of Journalism, Media and Communication Conference in 2026, bringing together researchers, academics and media practitioners to examine issues including artificial intelligence, disinformation, fact-checking, media ownership, business models and journalism education. Its research ambitions received another boost through the Africa Learning for Ethical Response to Truth Distortion (ALeRT) project, a three-year Erasmus+ initiative involving international and African partner institutions. UniMAC has been allocated €83,106.90 under the project and will lead a work package focused on implementing and steering a blended course addressing fact-checking, media literacy, artificial intelligence awareness and disinformation. The university’s relationship with industry has also become an important part of its development agenda. One notable partnership is with Dentsu Ghana, which collaborated with the Institute of Film and Television to refurbish its animation, multimedia and radio studios. The intervention included upgrades to the radio studio and two creative rooms, alongside the donation of 15 computers, five Wacom tablets, a camera, lenses, a gimbal stabiliser, microphones, headsets and an uninterruptible power supply system. Other collaborations include professional communication and record-keeping training delivered to 300 staff members of Komfo Anokye Teaching Hospital through the Institute of Languages. The university also signed a memorandum of understanding with Sputnik News Agency in Russia to strengthen media cooperation between the two countries, while its international engagements have created opportunities for student exchanges and professional exposure. Four students were selected for exchange programmes at NLA University College and Volda University College in Norway, while nine others participated in a Collaborative Online International Learning programme with the University of the Fraser Valley in Canada. Two journalism students, Titus Owusu Darko and Precious Akos Agrobesa, also won the 2026 Commonwealth Parliamentary Association National Debate Competition and subsequently represented Ghana at the international competition in Sydney, Australia. On infrastructure, Professor Mensah disclosed that the university was working towards improving its digital and physical learning environment. A 400-bed student hostel under construction at its East Legon campus is expected to help address accommodation needs, while a Student Records Management System, which is currently 90 per cent complete, is expected to be ready by December 2026. The system is intended to improve admissions, student administration, lecture hall management and course management while reducing reliance on manual records. However, the Vice-Chancellor acknowledged that infrastructure investment, technology acquisition, human resource requirements and the need to keep academic programmes relevant to rapidly changing industries continued to place pressure on the university. He appealed to corporate Ghana and industry players to regard UniMAC as a strategic partner in developing the country’s media and creative economy, arguing that the institution had the expertise, programmes and human capacity to contribute meaningfully to national development. Graduation statistics and outstanding performers Of the 1,414 graduands, 1,224 came from the Institute of Journalism, representing 86.56 per cent of the class. The Institute of Languages accounted for 117 graduates, representing 8.27 per cent, while the Institute of Film and Television produced 73 graduates, representing 5.16 per cent. Women constituted the majority, with 1,059 female graduates, compared with 355 males. In terms of academic classification, 200 students obtained first-class honours, 699 graduated with second-class upper division, 372 obtained second-class lower division, 115 received third-class honours, while 28 graduated with pass classifications. Among the outstanding performers was Calvin Dzomeku, who emerged as valedictorian and overall best graduating student with a cumulative grade point average of 3.99. He received the overall best graduating student award, sponsored by Fidelity Bank, with a GH¢10,000 prize. He also received the best student award for the School of Journalism and Media, sponsored by the Melcom Group of Companies in honour of its late Chairman, Bhagwan Ramchand Khubchandani. Other award recipients included Angela Bamford, who was recognised as the best student in the Faculty of Business and Strategic Communication and the best graduating female student, with a CGPA of 3.94. Precious Akos Agrobesa received the best student award in the Faculty of Communication and Liberal Studies, while Sandra Boamah was recognised as the best student in the Faculty of Cinematic and Television Arts. Yao Cedric Koudayah received the best student award in the Faculty of Digital Media and Design, while Bernice Tay Aku emerged as the best student in Translation and Bilingual Business Studies. The awards were supported by corporate partners including Brand Alert, Stanbic Bank, Farmhouse Productions, Apex Advertising, Ondo Health and Safety, Graphic Communications Group, YFM, Prudential Bank, the Lebanese Embassy and Fidelity Bank. Valedictorian urges graduates to focus on impact In his valedictory address, Mr Dzomeku offered a candid reflection on the experiences of the graduating class, acknowledging the academic demands, group assignments, competing ideas and sacrifices that shaped their university journey. He said the journey began on 16 January 2023 and concluded on 16 August 2026, describing the experience as one that had tested students academically, socially and personally. He recalled the demanding nature of assignments and lectures, jokingly drawing on the popular social media expression, “Yakubu, manage!” to describe how students had persevered through difficult periods. However, he said those experiences had ultimately helped shape their discipline, resilience and ability to work with people holding different perspectives. His most significant message concerned the uncertainty awaiting graduates beyond the university environment. “Life has no examination timetable, no prescribed syllabus and certainly no special consideration for late submissions,” he said, urging his colleagues to approach the world of work with patience, determination and a willingness to learn. He also appealed to university management to improve lecture hall facilities and the student portal, particularly its registration and results-processing systems, saying the improvements would benefit continuing students and graduates who might return for postgraduate studies. Acknowledging the financial sacrifices made by parents, guardians and sponsors, he specifically thanked the Lebanese Scholarship Scheme for investing in students’ education. He urged the graduating class to measure success not simply by the qualifications they had earned but by the solutions they would provide to society’s problems. “Our success will not be measured merely by the certificates we carry, but by the problems we solve and the lives we impact,” he said. Professor Mensah reinforced that message with five pieces of advice to the graduates, urging them to distinguish visibility from value, create rather than merely follow trends, understand audiences instead of chasing algorithms, become voices rather than noise, and remain curious, creative and relevant. UniMAC’s history and institutional mandate The congregation also offered a glimpse into the institution’s wider historical significance. UniMAC was established under the University of Media, Arts and Communication Act, 2020 (Act 1059), bringing together three institutions with longstanding contributions to Ghana’s educational and professional landscape: the Ghana Institute of Journalism, established in 1959; the Ghana Institute of Languages, established in 1961; and the National Film and Television Institute, established in 1978. The merger brought their complementary disciplines under one university, creating an institution with a mandate extending across the production, interpretation, preservation and communication of knowledge. For a university established to bring together some of Ghana’s longstanding specialist institutions in media, film and languages, the challenge is increasingly to ensure that its academic training keeps pace with an industry where creativity, technology, professional judgement and entrepreneurship are becoming closely intertwined. With its first Chancellor now in office, a new strategic plan in operation and a growing number of graduates entering the labour market, UniMAC faces the task of translating its academic strengths into greater opportunities for Ghana’s creative industries. For the 1,414 graduates, the ceremony marked the conclusion of one academic chapter. For the university, it was a reminder that its influence will ultimately be measured by the quality of professionals it produces and the contribution they make to Ghana and the wider world.

items.title: Tyson Fury diagnosed with schizophrenia
items.description: Tyson Fury says he was diagnosed with schizophrenia soon after his world title win over Wladimir Klitschko in 2015. British heavyweight Fury, 38, says he heard voices in his head threatening to hurt him and his family. In a documentary which will be released by Netflix on Friday, Fury and wife Paris describe how he was diagnosed after being admitted to hospital with a suspected heart attack in June 2016. “Words can’t explain the darkness I was in,” Fury says. “It was like a living version of the pits of hell. I thought I would end up in a padded room with the door locked, and that scared me so much. “The anxiety was crippling me. I just could not overcome it and that’s when I went and saw the psychiatrist down in London. She asked me a gazillion questions, and I ticked all the boxes. Depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder.” Doctors said Fury had suffered an anxiety attack. Fury recalls hearing the radio talking to him, and begging Paris to get him out of the hospital because “the Illuminati” wanted him. In the period after his victory over Klitschko, Fury gained weight and struggled with drug and alcohol addiction. “It got that bad I was hearing voices in my mind,” he says. “I wouldn’t be able to sit and have a conversation because I’d be hearing stuff in my mind. “I didn’t know where to turn and no one knew what to do. I really needed help, or check into rehab or something. “I never got a break from it for years. I wanted to be what I thought was normal again.” After Fury was released from hospital, a diagnosis of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder was confirmed, according to the documentary. The NHS describes schizophrenia as a form of psychosis, and symptoms can include hallucinations, delusions and muddled thoughts and speech. It says the main symptom of bipolar disorder is extreme changes to your mood. Fury describes a “turning point” in 2017 when he was on a night out for Halloween. “I went out and I was embarrassed by how I looked,” he says. “I was a fat mess and I had a glow-in-the-dark skeleton suit with full face mask on. “I looked around and could see all the young people and I thought, ‘I had the world in my hands and I threw it all away, and now I’m a fat mess addicted to alcohol’.” He says that was the beginning of a comeback which led him to focus more on his family and to return to training. It resulted in another world title when he beat Deontay Wilder in 2020. Fury is preparing for the long-awaited all-British heavyweight fight against Anthony Joshua in Cardiff on 11 December. The fight will be broadcast live on Netflix.

items.title: Petrol price reduced by Rs3 per litre; diesel remains unchanged
items.description: The government on Monday reduced the price of petrol by Rs3 per litre while keeping that of diesel unchanged at Rs357 per litre, after snapping a 12-day streak of consecutive reductions in the rate of petrol the previous week. Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs319 per litre on Nov 24 (Tuesday), according to a notification by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra). The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. Under an arrangement announced on Nov 2, for 30 days, oil refineries will contribute to the petroleum levy by bearing a cumulative impact of Rs15 billion, according to the government. This allows a Rs14.71 reduction in the petrol price at the consumer end. On Sept 17, the government rolled out the Prime Minister’s Fuel Relief Scheme across the country to ease the public’s burden amid rising fuel prices due to the Middle East situation. The subsidy scheme applies to owners of motorcycles, rickshaws and vehicles of up to 800cc. Rise in fuel prices The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on Feb 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm, and fuel allocations for official vehicles have been cut by 50pc for three months. Since July 17 , the government has been revising fuel prices on a near-daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give Ogra the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the conflict. The federal government had also announced targeted relief measures in April to provide subsidised fuel. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and HSD are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

items.title: Coopération militaire Burkina-Mali : Des officiers stagiaires burkinabè en immersion auprès des institutions militaires maliennes
items.description: Les officiers stagiaires de la 2e promotion de l'École d'État-major du Burkina Faso ont effectué, le vendredi 20 novembre 2026, une série de visites auprès de plusieurs institutions militaires maliennes, dans le cadre de leur voyage d'études au Mali. L'information est rendue publique par les Forces armées maliennes. La délégation s'est notamment rendue à la Direction des écoles militaires, à l'État-major général des Armées et au ministère de la Défense et des anciens combattants. Ces visites avaient pour objectif de familiariser les stagiaires avec l'organisation, le fonctionnement et les missions des différentes structures militaires du Mali. À l'État-major général des Armées, ils ont été reçus par le chef d'État-major général des Armées, le général de division Élysée Jean Dao. Les échanges ont notamment porté sur l'opération « Dougoukoloko » et les différentes formes de menaces sécuritaires auxquelles le Mali, le Burkina Faso et le Niger sont confrontés. Les discussions ont ainsi permis d'aborder les enjeux sécuritaires communs aux trois pays. La délégation a également été reçue par le ministre délégué auprès du ministre de la Défense et des anciens combattants, le général de division Oumar Diarra. Les échanges ont porté, a ce niveau, sur l'évolution de la situation sécuritaire au Mali, ainsi que sur la montée en puissance de la Force unifiée de la Confédération des États du Sahel (AES). Ces visites témoignent de la volonté de renforcer les liens entre les institutions militaires des pays membres de la Confédération AES. Elles constituent également un cadre de partage d'expériences et de consolidation de la coopération militaire face aux défis sécuritaires communs. Lefaso.net Source : Forces armées maliennes

items.title: The President Is Acting Like He Works for China
items.description: Americans learned several things over the past few days. The most recent news is that Jensen Huang, after a nanosecond of disgrace for an affair with a woman allegedly connected to Chinese intelligence , is back in control of Nvidia, the giant corporation that makes some of the world’s most advanced AI chips. Another is that China’s Communist regime has gotten its hands on the chips. The markets, as usual, have reconfirmed that they prefer profit to politics: Nvidia’s stock price jumped more than 30 percent on the news of Huang’s return. But most important, Americans learned—yet again—that their president does not care about the national security of the United States. In fact, he is so aggressively resistant to any notion of security that his actions have become almost indistinguishable from those of a hostile foreign agent. Step back for a moment and consider this sequence of events. The married Nvidia boss was caught in a sexual relationship with a woman named Alice Huang. (She is not related to Jensen, but I will use first names here to avoid confusion). Alice, during this affair, worked for Megaspeed, a company in Singapore. Megaspeed bought Nvidia chips, and then found ways to get them to China, despite U.S. export controls. She also reportedly maintained contacts with the Ministry of State Security, the Chinese intelligence agency, while carrying on with Jensen. (Some reports call Alice an “agent” or a “spy,” others refer to her as an “asset.” The distinction makes little practical difference in Jensen’s case. An agent is someone who is employed by an intelligence agency, has professional training, and may be acting under a false identity. An asset is someone in private life who has a cooperative relationship with such an agency but isn’t actually employed as a spook. Either way, Jensen was literally in bed with someone who was reportedly in bed with Chinese intelligence.) [ Josh Tyrangiel: Three theories of Jensen Huang’s resurrection ] All of this certainly looks bad. It gets worse. The United States government, including President Trump, was warned by American intelligence that Alice was entangled with Beijing. In fact, Trump was warned twice in seven months, including once during a briefing by Marco Rubio aboard Air Force One in May as Trump was headed to China for a state visit. This must have been awkward, because shortly afterward, Jensen Huang boarded Air Force One and joined the U.S. delegation for the trip to China. Trump ignored these warnings—or more accurately, in classic Trump style, he pretended not to know about these issues. “I’d certainly check with the intelligence people,” he said, just before his most recent visit to China. “They could have been mentioned. Certainly, it didn’t make much of an impact on me.” Clearly not. Nor did these warnings move Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, whose former company, Cantor Fitzgerald, has significant ties to Nvidia , including financing some of the firms that were buying its chips. The company is now run by Lutnick’s son. Trump’s reaction to all this? When Jensen was discovered and had to leave his company, Trump got right to work trying to put him back in the big chair at Nvidia. “I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance. You know, we’re a country of second chances.” Nvidia wasn’t having it : Internal sources at the company made clear to reporters that Jensen Huang would not be reinstated. So what changed in a matter of days? Nothing, except that the president apparently brought the American intelligence community into the fray to give Jensen a clean bill of health. At least that’s how it sounds from the Nvidia board’s public statement: “In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” The national-security process is slow and deliberative for a reason; people with even modest clearances who have been accused of minor infractions have had to wait months, sometimes even going to court, before being allowed back to work. An executive working with some of America’s most exotic technology commits adultery with a foreign citizen who has ties to a hostile government, and is credibly accused of funneling highly restricted American technology to a hostile intelligence service—and the U.S. security mandarins give the guy a thumbs up after a week ? Trump likes Jensen, he likes money, he likes the markets, and he likes Lutnick and his family. So perhaps he told the American spooks to sound the all-clear so that Jensen could get back to work. Trump indicated as much today when he told CNBC that he spoke with Nvidia’s board members. “I spoke to them, let me put it that way. And I convinced them.” In a statement on Truth Social, Trump said: “The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.” That means exactly nothing. Saying that Todd Blanche does not “possess evidence” is an artful formulation meaning that Blanche does not have a file in front of him from the intelligence community detailing Jensen’s acts, some of which might have been dangerous even if they were not “unlawful.” (As any government employee can tell you, any number of “lawful” activities, including carrying lots of debt or having emotional problems, can sink a clearance and a job.) And because of Trump’s pressure to clear Jensen, it’s unlikely he ever will. Not only did Trump celebrate the Nvidia decision, but he noted that the board’s action possibly averted a worse outcome: Jensen Huang working for China. If Jensen was “mad” enough, Trump said during an interview today , he might have accepted an offer to lead a Chinese company, because the Nvidia boss has some of their “blood in him.” In other words, the United States just vouched for a man the president said might have defected to China if he hadn’t been given his job back. [ Jonathan Chait: Trump’s backing of Huang is not superintelligent ] To recap: After a top industrialist got caught in an affair with a woman who might have been using the affair to slip American technology to a U.S. enemy, the president declared that his own spies had cleared his pal, waved off the national-security damage, and left everyone, ostensibly, happy. And by “everyone,” I mean Jensen Huang, Howard Lutnick, Nvidia stockholders, and Communist China. Trump solved this problem in a way that would make a foreign spy or a lobbyist for a foreign government both impressed and envious. Enemy spooks, their agents, and their assets spend their lives trying to do what Trump did in a week. Jensen’s off the hook, and the stock has bounced back. (And the Chinese should give Alice a medal.) This whole terrible situation shows in galling detail that Trump just doesn’t think very much about the interests of the United States. (It also suggests that he couldn’t care less about the recent election, in which corruption was a top issue for many voters). He makes no secret of his preference for his own relationships over America’s safety: When asked if Russian President Vladimir Putin was a “friend to America,” Trump shrugged and said, “I can’t speak to America. ” That’s because Trump, for all his flag-hugging nonsense, doesn’t think in terms of “America” or “China” or “Russia.” He is a globalist, in the very worst sense of the word: a man who cares nothing for states or peoples or ideologies, because he sees the world as just an interconnected group of companies and banks. Some of those companies are run by his friends, and those are the only peers who matter. Everyone else is just raw material or collateral damage; the masses are just ciphers who either obey him or obey someone else. It is perhaps an insult to foreign agents to say that Trump is acting like them. Foreign agents work for countries, and care about them. They do what they do out of patriotism, however misguided they may be about the regimes they might serve. Trump has no such ideals. Trump’s business is Trump’s business, and everything else—including “national interest” and “national security”—are just meaningless phrases used by chumps and saps.

items.title: AES, la paix sans capitulation…
items.description: Les pays de l’Alliance des États du Sahel doivent regarder la réalité en face. La crise sécuritaire ne saurait être expliquée uniquement par le djihadisme. Elle comporte également une dimension géopolitique, marquée par des rivalités de puissances, des intérêts stratégiques et de graves accusations d’ingérence étrangère. La France doit répondre des accusations portées contre elle. Le 15 août 2022, le Mali a officiellement saisi le Conseil de sécurité des Nations unies, dans une lettre référencée S/2022/622, accusant la France de violations de son espace aérien, de collecte de renseignements au profit de groupes terroristes et de largages d’armes et de munitions. Le 30 septembre 2024, à la tribune de la 79e Assemblée générale des Nations unies, le ministre nigérien des Affaires étrangères, Bakary Yaou Sangaré, a expressément accusé la France de renseigner, former, financer et armer des groupes terroristes au Sahel. Ces accusations ont été reprises au plus haut niveau par Son Excellence Ali Mahaman Lamine ZEINE, Premier ministre du Niger, lors de son intervention du 26 septembre 2026 devant la 81e Assemblée générale. Il a dénoncé une entreprise française de déstabilisation et qualifié la situation sahélienne d’entreprise de recolonisation. Ces accusations, rejetées par Paris, ne peuvent être balayées d’un revers de main. Elles exigent des investigations internationales sérieuses. Après plus d’une décennie d’interventions militaires occidentales, notamment l’opération Barkhane lancée en août 2014 et achevée au Mali en 2022, le bilan sécuritaire et les responsabilités extérieures doivent être examinés sans complaisance. Les chiffres donnent la mesure du drame. Selon le Global Terrorism Index 2026, le Niger a enregistré 944 décès liés au terrorisme en 2024, contre 703 en 2025, ainsi que 88 incidents terroristes en 2025. Le pays occupe le troisième rang mondial des pays les plus touchés. Derrière ces chiffres, il y a des familles endeuillées, des villages traumatisés et des populations privées de sécurité. Dans ce contexte, pourquoi accorder une légitimité politique aux directions des organisations armées ? Le JNIM et l’État islamique au Sahel disposent de réseaux transnationaux, de financements et de stratégies territoriales. Ces organisations poursuivent des objectifs idéologiques et territoriaux qui dépassent largement les revendications locales. Les frustrations communautaires doivent être traitées, mais elles ne justifient ni les massacres ni les projets de domination armée. L’AES doit consolider ses alliances régionales. L’excellente relation entre le Niger et l’Algérie constitue à cet égard un atout stratégique. La visite de fraternité et de travail du Président Abdourahamane Tiani en Algérie, les 15 et 16 février 2026, a réaffirmé la solidité des relations entre les deux pays. Les deux États ont convenu de renforcer le contrôle de leurs frontières et la coordination de leurs stratégies de lutte contre le terrorisme. Les 23 et 24 mars 2026, la deuxième session de la Grande Commission mixte nigéro-algérienne, tenue à Niamey, a confirmé leur volonté d’élever ce partenariat à un niveau stratégique. La négociation politique avec les directions des organisations terroristes comporte des risques majeurs. Les contacts humanitaires destinés à sauver des vies restent possibles, mais ils ne doivent pas devenir une reconnaissance politique de groupes qui imposent leur autorité par la terreur. La souveraineté du Sahel ne se négocie pas sous la menace. L’AES doit renforcer ses capacités militaires, son renseignement, sa coopération régionale et son indépendance diplomatique. Elle doit également exiger que les responsabilités de toute puissance impliquée dans une éventuelle entreprise de déstabilisation soient établies. Le Sahel n’a pas besoin d’une nouvelle tutelle ni d’une paix qui consacrerait les résultats de la violence. Il a besoin de sécurité, de justice et de maîtrise de son propre destin. Les peuples du Sahel ne doivent plus payer le prix des rivalités géopolitiques et des ambitions des puissances étrangères. Par Ousmane Jazy L’article AES, la paix sans capitulation… est apparu en premier sur Tamtaminfo .

items.title: Bayelsa boat mishap death toll rises to 32, AIG visits scene
items.description: …Urges enforcement of life jacket, passenger capacity regulations By Samuel Oyadongha, Yenagoa The Assistant Inspector-General of Police in charge of Zone 16, Regina Udoette, has visited Ayama-Ijaw waterside in Southern Ijaw Local Government Area of Bayelsa State following the boat mishap that claimed 32 lives. Udoette, who was accompanied by the Bayelsa State Commissioner of Police, Saka Ajao Adewale, visited the area on Monday to interact with marine transport workers and the Red Cross rescue team and receive updates on the ongoing search and recovery operation. During the visit, reports from the rescue site indicated that additional bodies had been recovered, raising the death toll from 29 to 32. The AIG commiserated with the Bayelsa State Government and residents over the tragedy, while commending President Bola Tinubu for his response and expression of sympathy following the incident. She expressed concern over alleged violations of maritime safety regulations, particularly the overloading of the vessel and failure to comply with life jacket requirements. According to her, the boat reportedly conveyed more than 500 passengers despite having a carrying capacity of 200. Udoette urged the state Ministry of Transport and marine unions to strengthen enforcement of safety regulations, particularly compulsory life jacket use and compliance with approved passenger limits. She also called for strict enforcement against operators who flout safety rules, stressing that passengers must take personal responsibility for their safety. Speaking with journalists, the AIG said she visited the waterside on behalf of the Inspector-General of Police to sympathise with the victims’ families and assess the situation. “I am here with my management team and the Bayelsa CP on behalf of the Inspector General of Police to sympathise with the people that died in the incident. I register our condolences and wish the injured quick recovery. “Besides, the maritime personnel told us of the refusal of passengers to obey safety rules, and the boat captain loaded over 500 persons for a boat with a 200-person capacity. That was a suicide mission and a disaster waiting to happen,” she said. Describing the deaths as avoidable, Udoette urged passengers and marine transport operators to comply with established safety regulations. “Some of these deaths are avoidable deaths. Many of the passengers refuse to obey safety rules. My Bible tells me obedience is better than sacrifice. There are rules and regulations on life jackets and overloading, but they refused. “For the living, this is a big lesson to everyone that wants to use a boat for their journey. They should listen to the rules. People should use common sense. This disaster is avoidable,” she added. The post Bayelsa boat mishap death toll rises to 32, AIG visits scene appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Nigeria records 94% HIV viral suppression – NACA
items.description: The NACA director-general, however, identified gaps in HIV diagnosis, stressing the need to ensure more Nigerians know their status and access uninterrupted treatment. She said Early Infant Diagnosis coverage among HIV-exposed infants increased from 15 per cent in 2022 to 66 per cent in 2025. “While this is significant progress, we must do more to ensure that no child is left behind,” Ilori said. She said the 2026 World AIDS Day theme, “Ending AIDS Starts with Access: Equity, Ownership and Sustainability,” highlighted the need for equitable access to HIV prevention, testing, treatment and care. “Access must not depend on where you live, what you earn or who you are. It is a right, not a privilege,” she said. Ilori announced that NACA would unveil the National HIV Domestic Resource Mobilisation and Sustainability Strategy 2026–2030 on Dec. 1, as part of the World AIDS Day commemoration. According to her, the strategy will strengthen domestic financing, promote national ownership and sustain Nigeria’s HIV response amid declining global health funding. She also announced plans for a National Prevention Conference to explore innovative HIV prevention approaches, including self-testing, pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) and emerging prevention technologies. Dr Adebobola Bashorun, National Coordinator, National AIDS, Viral Hepatitis and STIs Control Programme (NASCP), said innovations would only save lives if they were accessible and affordable. “We can have the best technology and products, but without access they are useless,” he said. Bashorun said Nigeria was scaling up injectable HIV prevention medicines, oral PrEP and interventions to prevent mother-to-child transmission. UNAIDS Country Director, Ms Tina Boonto, said more than 1.5 million Nigerians living with HIV were accessing antiretroviral treatment. She, however, said Nigeria recorded about 64,000 new HIV infections annually, far above the fewer than 5,000 required to end AIDS as a public health threat. “Ending AIDS starts with ensuring everyone can access the services, medicines, technologies and information they need,” she said. Boonto called for increased HIV testing, expanded prevention services and stronger efforts to eliminate mother-to-child transmission. Dr Patrick Dakum, Executive Officer, Institute for Human Virology (IHVN), represented by the Director of Prevention, Care and Treatment, Dr Helen Omuh, stressed the need for equitable access to HIV services, community ownership and sustained domestic commitment. Dakum, speaking on behalf of implementing partners, reaffirmed their commitment to expanding effective interventions, strengthening domestic ownership and financing, and promoting sustainability. “We want to affirm that ending AIDS requires more than service availability. It requires equitable access, empowered communities, strong national ownership and sustainable investment. “So together, we can build a resilient HIV response and accelerate Nigeria’s progress towards ending AIDS as a public health threat,” he said. Mr Nicholas Ugbenyen, National Secretary, Network of People Living with HIV/AIDS in Nigeria (NEPWHAN), expressed confidence that access, equity, community ownership and sustainability would help Nigeria end AIDS. Mrs Esther Hindi, National Coordinator, Association of Women Living with HIV/AIDS (ASHWAN), called for stronger efforts to prevent mother-to-child transmission. “For us and for every pregnant woman out there carrying a baby, we say prevention is better than cure. “We need to protect our unborn children from HIV so that they can have a strong future,” she said.
