items.title: Why I Changed My Mind About the Death Penalty
items.description: We had to crawl . We were warned not to lift our faces. We had to press our noses to the floor. The hotel was cheap and the carpet stank. The TV was on but we did not hear it, because we were listening for commands. There was a man standing over us while we crawled. He was telling us where to go. He was ordering us to crawl to the bathtub, and he had a gun, a very big one, the single legible shadow in a situation of enforced blindness. The bathtub was a surprise, the second in a series. The first was his presence in the room. We were salesmen, on the road. It was night, and I had gone to my colleague Steven’s room to drink whiskey and smoke pot and watch television. I had made a mistake and left the door to the room ajar, and while I was taking a piss, a gun barrel nipped the flesh of my temple and turned my head at an angle from my shoulders. I was marched like that, like a marionette, back into the room, where Steven was sitting on the bed with his back propped against the headboard. He tried to move backwards, as if pedaling on a bicycle, but the headboard stopped him. His expression changed five times until it settled into a kind of antic sadness, like the mask of tragedy. The man with the gun—the robber, the thief, the gunman, the intruder, I still don’t know what to call him—made us lie on the bed, our faces in the pillows. He stayed a long time, asking us questions and letting us know that lies would carry mortal consequence. He thought we were hiding money. “You’re not lying to me, are you? You better not be.” For a while, we passed the test. Then something changed, and he told us to get on the floor and crawl. The bathtub was small and cold and hard to climb into from our prostration on the bathroom floor, especially with someone assuring us that he would kill us if we looked at his face. How could we not look at his face? I looked at his face when I looked at the gun. He had a dapper pointed mustache and he was sweating profusely and the round hole at the end of the long barrel was somehow blacker than the gun itself, somehow more absolute. “I told you not to look at me,” he said, and it was the reasonableness of his voice that made everything speed up, that made me want to cling to every passing moment. He told Steven to turn the tap and run the water and Steven, instead, folded his hands before him and said, “Oh, Jesus Christ, please don’t kill us.” The man behind the gun responded with seeming annoyance: “Don’t ‘Jesus’ me. I’m a God-fearing motherfucker myself.” I worried that the annoyance would be fatal but when I looked at him again, the gun was no longer the empty eye staring at my head. He lifted the barrel, told us not to call the cops for another 15 minutes, and left. We did not wait 15 minutes. The cops came, and treated it, at first, as just another hotel-room holdup. But one detail mystified the lead investigator. He had been to many crime scenes in his life, but usually when people were forced into a bathtub at gunpoint they did not get out. “What happened to them?” I asked, for I was 22 years old, until that moment still a boy. “They were executed,” he said. “Putting you in the bathtub is an execution scenario.” An execution scenario—so that was it. That was what had happened. I couldn’t quite bring myself to say it, but once the word execution spelled itself out in my brain, it stayed there, a tightly knotted cord, a hangman’s noose, forever. I, along with Steven, had been put through the paces of execution. I had survived being put through the paces of execution. [ Elizabeth Bruenig: The woman who has prevented 200 executions ] When a detective called two months later with the news that the man who robbed us had been arrested, the first question I asked was “Did he kill anyone?” The detective demurred; he said, “You don’t have to worry about that,” because the sweaty gunman with the dapper mustache had robbed so many salesmen in so many marginal hotels that he didn’t need to bring me in to testify. I never got the answer to my question. Nor did I think to get the man’s name. But there existed for many years an alternative version of events in which he did kill someone, in which Steven didn’t invoke the Lord’s name and I wound up as splash and splatter in a hotel bathtub. I was fired from my sales job shortly after the detective’s call. I began writing, and the first thing I wrote about was what had happened in the hotel room, and what I’d had to surrender, in terms of will. I also began thinking about the other kind of execution, the state-sanctioned practice we call the death penalty. I made a decision about it, and the decision surprised me. I had grown up Catholic, at a time when the pro-life Church placed nearly as much emphasis on opposing the death penalty and euthanasia as it did on abortion. But I approved of the death penalty. I couldn’t call myself an advocate, or even a proponent. I just believed in the essential rightness of it, because I knew that life or death is a decision—because I knew, with the certainty of experience, that the man who’d exiled me to a bathtub and pointed a gun at my head had not only the power of life and death, but the power of choice. He was not in a rush, he was not making his getaway, he was not panicking, he didn’t seem at all afraid. He had held us captive for nearly 45 minutes, and then he decided whether to kill us or let us live. It was my memory of his deliberation, the icy luxury of time on his hands, that formed the rationale for my belief that the death penalty was not murder, but a necessary answer to murder. Had he taken our lives, he would have chosen to deny us mercy—and so to him mercy must be denied. I didn’t believe in the efficacy of the death penalty as a deterrent. I believed that anyone who decides to kill has also decided to be killed. I believed that murder is an eternal crime that must be punished in kind. I was not proud of this belief, but I held on to it as it held on to me. I kept it in some secret stash of my soul when I wrote, back in the ’90s, about a jailbird hipster who had been sentenced to death for murdering a Domino’s employee named John Collins. I’d gotten to know Tony Mobley. In the course of interviewing him, I asked him what it was like to kill a man. He made it sound like a rare thrill. He also showed me the word DOMINO proudly tattooed on his shoulder, a mark that carried the force of a biblical stain. I was grateful to him for his honesty, and that made it awkward to admit to myself—though never to him—that I thought the jury had ultimately made the right call. But 10 years after I met him, I still went down to the big state penitentiary south of Atlanta and kept vigil just outside the gates on the night he was supposed to die. I did not go as a reporter. I drove to the prison on a whim, a sudden pang of guilt and curiosity and obligation, the first and only time I put myself in the vicinity of a government execution. It was cloudy and cold and damp, a night of continual shivers. There were a few people on hand, most of them members of a death-row ministry, praying. I didn’t know if anyone was inside, for Tony. I knew that members of the Collins family had declined to attend; they had asked the state to spare the man who’d killed John—because killing Tony wouldn’t bring him back. I drank coffee to keep warm and I waited. But for what? I had always viewed the death penalty from the perspective of my own crouching helplessness in the bathtub, the endless instants that passed with my life in another’s hands. Now I was waiting outside a prison where, somewhere inside, a person I knew was being strapped down and killed. I was waiting for news that the killing had been successful, and I was drinking coffee. Tony Mobley died at 8 p.m. on March 1, 2005. He had withheld mercy from John Collins and mercy had been withheld from him. And yet when the prison spokesman emerged from behind the gates to say that the sentence had been carried out and justice had been done, I did not feel that something had been set aright, that the scales had been balanced. I began asking a question so obvious, it embarrassed me. If my experience on my knees in a bathtub told me that the great sin of murder was not just the taking of a life but the cold, rational, deliberative process that led to it, how was what had just happened anything less than murderous? The death penalty is not an impersonal manifestation of karmic justice; it must be “administered” by fallible human beings working for an even more fallible system that labors under the pretense of blind and impartial judgment. What gives us the right? What gives anyone the right? As much as part of my soul cried out for the satisfaction of the death penalty, the answer that came to me is that we don’t have the right. We do not live in a pro-life country, and I am aware that for some readers, my argument against the death penalty for a murderer with DOMINO printed on his shoulder will sound less convincing than my argument for it. We do not, as a people, like to look at how we kill our killers. We especially don’t like to face up to the racial disparities of death row and the growing body of evidence suggesting that the innocent have died along with the guilty. But every so often we have the chance to see how very personal the impersonal machinations of capital punishment really are, with the lies and the pieties stripped away. This happened recently, when Christa Pike, paying for her part in the torture and murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, went into the death chamber in Tennessee, and somehow came out alive. She was put through the paces of execution, but the drugs injected into her arm while she was strapped to the gurney failed to kill her, and so, as the state of Tennessee sought to answer murder with murder, it wound up answering torture with torture . As of this writing, we don’t know if it will try to kill her again, but that haze of indecision did not stop Senator Marsha Blackburn from using her successful run for governor to declare that what Pike’s failed execution really proves is that we ought to “bring back the electric chair.” Torture, then, is not enough; we have to smell the burning scalp. Nobody likes to think of themselves as bloodthirsty. I certainly did not like to think of myself as bloodthirsty when I supported the death penalty, only as realistic, rational, and in favor of cosmic reckonings. But, around the same time Pike lived to die another day, “Secretary of War” Pete Hegseth did us the favor of being openly bloodthirsty, and counting on the rest of America to be equally forthright. He came up with the idea that if what the mass murderer Nidal Hasan needed was execution by military firing squad, then what America needed was to watch it , “on streaming.” He sought to shore up our flagging national resolve, but his actual achievement was to elicit what has been so hard to come by for the past 10 years: our shame. [ Elizabeth Bruenig: Public execution won’t have the effect Trump intends ] Is shame the right word for what subsequently compelled Governor Gavin Newsom to commute the sentences of all 548 prisoners on California’s death row? It isn’t, although Newsom reportedly saw the Christa Pike debacle as an opportunity to press forward with a moral argument that, of necessity, will become a political one. He wrote, in his letter announcing the decision , that “state-sanctioned killing” is something that “diminishes each of us.” It is a powerful letter, confident in its sweep: “Many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die. But as governor, I have concluded the state cannot morally kill them.” The absolutism of that last sentence made me think of the bathtub, and the beliefs that followed me out of it. Am I ashamed of the conviction that resulted from coming face-to-face with a shiny black .45, which spoke of nothing more eloquently than my own death? I am not, in part because if I am honest with myself, I have to say that I have no idea what shape my convictions would take if a member of my family died in an “execution scenario” or, for that matter, in a random act of violence. All I know is this: I survived. And I survived because I was spared. Was I spared because, as the cop on the scene suggested, my colleague Steven called upon Jesus Christ? I can’t say I wasn’t, but at the same time, my continued presence on this Earth was not and is not a miracle. I was spared because a human being spared me. [ From the December 2019 issue: Tom Junod on Mister Rogers’s enduring wisdom ] I will never know the name of the man who made me crawl, fire having consumed his police file long ago, and I don’t like to give him too much credit, in case he did execute someone else. But I had gotten the story wrong, and it led me for a time to the wrong conclusions. I always contended that had he killed me, he should in turn be killed, if only to demonstrate what my life was worth. But in fact he didn’t kill me. He had power over me—an absolute power I can’t contemplate without getting a little sick—and he lifted his gun. I will never know why. I can only state a truth still hard to say, because it obliges me to him. He terrorized me, and he took something from me, not only money. But my life began when he gave me something back. It is hard to think of a guy pointing a gun at your head as merciful, especially now, decades later, when mercy is in such short supply. But I am here both despite and because of him. I am here because he, a criminal, a villain, a robber, and possibly a murderer, was able to give me, in a moment of the most extreme exigency, something that is beyond so many death-state governors and Supreme Court justices deliberating matters of life and death at their leisure. I have marked the beginning of my life from the moment of my survival. I have lived more than 40 years past the bathtub. But I was, and remain, a child of mercy, old enough now to know that there are bathtubs everywhere, and mercy is all we’ve got. This article appears in the January 2027 print edition with the headline “An Execution Scenario.”

items.title: PTI's Zafar says Karachi can become separate province, Imran Khan favours new administrative units
items.description: ISLAMABAD: PTI parliamentary leader in the Senate, Barrister Ali Zafar, on Monday said that Karachi – Pakistan’s most populous metropolis – could be made a new province, claiming that party founder and former prime minister Imran Khan was in favour of it. However, Zafar stressed that it should be done in accordance with the Constitution, as the referendum, albeit constitutional, was only to seek the public’s opinion. Days ago, PTI’s Information Secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram had dismissed proposals for a referendum as an absurd and futile exercise that could not replace a majority vote or a constitutional bill in the national or provincial assemblies. The PML-N-led federal government has insisted on holding a referendum across the country on the establishment of new provinces or administrative units. However, the suggestion has faced severe backlash from its ally PPP. Speaking to the media outside Islamabad High Court on Monday, Zafar said the PTI was waiting for legislation on the creation of new provinces to be presented. “We will make our decision after analysing the draft of the 28th amendment,” he stated. While rumours of making changes to the Constitution have been circulating since at least May, a possible 28th amendment has not been officially proposed yet. Zafar said that the PTI founder had given a “straightforward instruction” regarding the formation of new provinces. “He (Imran) has said that as long as provinces are concerned, they should be made,” the PTI’s leader in the Senate said. However, Zafar cautioned that it should be observed how “they” want to make the provinces. “We will look into it – whether they want to violate the law or follow the law – and then will decide about it,“ he stated. “Khan sahib has said that whenever you get the draft, look into it […] and then come to me and share its pros and cons,” he added. While replying to a question, Barrister Zafar noted that a referendum was a constitutional way to get the opinion of the masses. However, he stressed that only public opinion could be sought through it and provinces must be created in the way “already mentioned in the Constitution ” — with the relevant provincial assembly’s consent. Turning to another question, Zafar said that PTI was a political party and the opinion of Imran would be sought if it is asked to vote on new provinces. Zafar said that while provinces could be established in Sindh, he personally believed that they should be made on an administrative basis rather than a linguistic basis. Moreover, he said it should be analysed whether those provinces can generate enough revenue and can be run on their own. “Karachi can be made a province. Similarly, interior Sindh and central Sindh can become provinces. In Punjab, south and north Punjab can become provinces. Similarly, in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the Hazara region can become a province,” he suggested. “We just want justice and if the government is ready to give justice, we are ready to talk about it,” he said, referring to the court orders related to shifting Imran to the hospital and providing access to his family and lawyers. The PTI has maintained that its founding chairman has consistently advocated for smaller administrative units; however, the party says it would never endorse decisions imposed without “constitutional legitimacy, democratic consensus, and public consent”. In September, PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan cautioned against making any “hasty decision” regarding the creation of new provinces, saying it would weaken the federation. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi has whipped up a political storm since July, when he called for the formation of new administrative units in the country, saying the current “system” of governance had “collapsed” and needed a “reset”. On Nov 12, Naqvi floated the idea of holding a referendum to gauge public opinion on the issue, saying the exercise could settle the contentious debate once and for all. Other federal ministers have also voiced their support for holding a referendum, with Defence Minister Khawaja Asif saying the process could likely move forward early next year.

items.description: (Kyon, le 21 novembre 2026) Dans le cadre de la lutte contre la fraude, les pratiques commerciales illicites et les atteintes aux droits des consommateurs, la Direction régionale de l’Industrie, du Commerce et de l’Artisanat de Nando (DRICA-NANDO) a conduit, hier samedi, une opération de contrôle dans la localité de Kyon, dans la province du Sanguié. Cette intervention a permis de contrôler 23 commerces, de sceller 11 établissements en infraction et de saisir plus d’une tonne de produits périmés et prohibés. Les contrôles effectués ont notamment révélé des manquements à la réglementation sur les prix ainsi que la commercialisation de produits périmés ou prohibés, impropres à la consommation ou interdits de vente. À travers cette opération, la DRICA-Nando entend assainir les circuits de commercialisation, lutter contre les pratiques frauduleuses et contribuer à la protection des consommateurs. Elle rappelle ainsi aux commerçants l'obligation de respecter les textes en vigueur. Les opérations de surveillance du marché se poursuivent dans la région de Nando. Les consommateurs sont également invités à signaler toute pratique commerciale irrégulière en appelant les numéros verts suivants : 80 00 11 84 / 80 00 11 85. items.title: Jamie Lee Curtis, en su cumpleaños número 68: “Es el primer año que soy la única superviviente de mi familia inmediata”
items.description: En la antesala del estreno de Una navidad de locos (2004), la actriz Jamie Lee Curtis (Los Ángeles, 68 años) perdió a su madre, Janet Leigh, protagonista del clásico Psicosis (1960) , por vasculitis. Su padre, Tony Curtis , falleció por un paro cardíaco en octubre de 2010, cuando estrenaba la comedia romántica ¿O tra vez tú? El pasado 30 de mayo, la hermana mayor de la actriz, Kelly Curtis, murió por causas naturales, lo que dejó a la protagonista de la saga de terror Halloween o Ponte en mi lugar como la única superviviente de su familia inmediata. Al cumplir los 68 años, la intérprete ha reflexionado en una publicación de este domingo en su cuenta de Instagram (con 6,7 millones de seguidores) sobre su primer cumpleaños sin la compañía de sus seres queridos más cercanos. “El largo y sinuoso camino. ¡Otra vuelta alrededor del sol! Hoy se cumple el primer año en el que soy la única superviviente de mi familia inmediata y de mi círculo familiar más cercano", inicia su mensaje, que acompaña de tres fotos en blanco y negro con su familia. items.title: French Bill Risks Deepening Police Impunity
items.description: Click to expand Image Protesters during a demonstration against the introduction of a presumption of legitimate use of weapons by police officers into French law in Paris, November 19, 2026. © 2026 Thibault Camus/AP Photo The French Senate on November 20 approved a controversial bill that risks deepening impunity for use of lethal force by police. The bill introduces a legal presumption of self-defense for law enforcement officers using firearms during the exercise of their duties, unless victims or their families can establish the use of lethal force was unlawful. Because victims’ families lack access to key evidence to assess the legality of police-caused death, placing the burden of proof on them is likely to deepen impunity and seriously jeopardize pathways for accountability where lethal force was unlawful, unnecessary, or disproportionate. This is inconsistent with France’s human rights obligations with respect to protecting the right to life and use of force by law enforcement. The use of lethal force by police is a major concern in France. In 2023, a police officer fatally shot 17-year-old Nahel M., a racialized boy, during a traffic stop, triggering widespread scrutiny of police use of firearms. France’s national human rights body and the previous mandate holder of the independent ombudsperson as well as a United Nations rights expert raised serious rights concerns about the bill, while rights groups, activists, and legal professionals staged protests and petitioned parliament to stop the bill. The Senate’s vote followed approval of the bill by France’s National Assembly on July 7. Unless government officials or parliamentarians refer the bill for constitutional review, the president has 15 days to sign it into law. Since 2017, when lawmakers broadened the scope of permissible use of firearms by police well beyond international human rights standards requiring necessity and proportionality, numbers of fatal police vehicle stops in France have risen fivefold compared to before. A state cannot delegate its legal duty to investigate to those affected by lethal police force. This reversed burden of proof contravenes international human rights law, which requires states to thoroughly investigate every circumstance of lethal police force. If the French authorities are serious about avoiding incidents of excessive use of lethal force, and rebuilding public confidence in policing, lawmakers should drop this bill. The government and parliament should instead focus legislative efforts on strengthening accountability and ensuring that police powers are subject to effective procedural safeguards to protect people from police abuse, discrimination, violence, and, increasingly, disproportionate use of firearms.

items.title: oPt: Palestine Logistics Cluster - Concept of Operations (ConOps) November, 2026
items.description: Country: occupied Palestinian territory Sources: Logistics Cluster, World Food Programme Please refer to the attached file. Background For the last 3 years the situation in Gaza has been marked by conflict, mass displacement, widespread infrastructure destruction and the collapse of essential services. The October 2025 ceasefire enabled some operational improvements but has not secured sustained humanitarian access or civilian safety. Continuing conflict, the activities of military and other armed groups, as well as continuing restrictions around demarcation lines threaten civilians, humanitarian personnel and logistics facilities, and impact access to affected communities. Needs remain extensive across food security, shelter, health and WASH sectors. Winter further compounds these needs: an estimated 294,250 families require shelter assistance, while approximately 950,000 displaced people live in sites at medium or high risk of flooding1 . Funding shortfalls are reducing assistance and limiting partners’ ability to replenish supplies, maintain operational capacity and prepare for seasonal emergencies. Humanitarian logistics remain constrained by heavily damaged infrastructure within Gaza, limited operational entry points into the Strip, complex clearance procedures (particularly for items considered “dual-use”), and intensive cargo inspections upstream. Cargo entering through the limited crossing points (at time of drafting only Kerem Shalom/Karem Abu Salem) depends on tightly coordinated movements; additional scanning, detailed inspections, and repeated handling slow down operations and can lead to delays, congestion and higher costs. Inside Gaza, damaged roads and warehouses, restricted routes, and limited access across the military demarcation line all constrain cargo collection, storage and onward distribution. Shortages of fuel, spare parts, lubricants and maintenance equipment undermine vehicle availability, while unreliable electricity and restrictions on equipment further compromise logistics operations. Airstrikes near warehouses, security incidents along key supply routes, and frequent checks and inspections further disrupt operations. Although transport markets in Jordan and Israel remain functional, substantial logistics gaps persist within Gaza. Predictable access, road rehabilitation, secure temporary storage, reliable transport and fuel, and coordinated cargo movements therefore remain essential to sustaining deliveries and reaching populations with lifesaving assistance at the scale required, particularly as winter conditions further impact operations.

items.title: North Kordofan: Alarm as Sheikh detained in El Obeid found dead
items.description: An elderly Sheikh has died in unexplained circumstances in El Obeid, North Kordofan, after being detained by a security force at a livestock market three days earlier. His body was subsequently found in the city’s morgue. The incident has raised serious concerns over alleged unlawful detention, torture, and extrajudicial killings, while the Kordofan Observatory has reported further cases of arbitrary detention and torture in the city. Multiple sources have confirmed the death of Sheikh Ali Abdelrahman El Kajjam, a man in his seventies, in the North Kordofan state capital of El Obeid. He died in mysterious circumstances after being detained by a security force at a livestock market north-east of the city three days earlier. His body was subsequently found in the morgue. Lawyer and human rights defender Osman Saleh told Radio Dabanga that Sheikh Ali Abdelrahman was a tribal leader and livestock trader who had been in good health and had suffered from no illnesses before his detention. Saleh cited eyewitness accounts saying that a group of uniformed security personnel wearing military clothing and travelling in a pickup truck arrived at the livestock market north-east of El Obeid. They called Sheikh Ali Abdelrahman by name and took him away along with two of his workers. “Inside El Obeid, the two workers were ordered out of the vehicle, beaten with rifle butts, and then released, while the sheikh was taken to an unknown destination,” he said. Saleh quoted family sources as saying that relatives began searching for Ali Abdelrahman on the same day he was detained. They approached police stations, military intelligence offices, the security cell, and National Intelligence and Security Service offices, but all denied having him in their custody. News subsequently spread on Sunday that a body had been found in the morgue. Members of the family identified it as that of Sheikh Ali Abdelrahman El Kajjam. Morgue officials reportedly said that uniformed personnel had brought the body and promised to return to complete the necessary procedures, but never came back. Legal violations Lawyer Osman Saleh described the incident as an unlawful abduction, saying that the force responsible had not identified itself, produced an arrest warrant, or taken the sheikh to a police station. He said police stations were the only legally authorised bodies to deal with civilians in matters of arrest and investigation. He held the state government directly and fully responsible for the security and safety of citizens. He described its failure to know which authority had detained the sheikh as a catastrophe, stressing that it bore full responsibility for his abduction, torture, and death. Saleh also raised questions about the responsibility of the morgue and hospital, saying that a body should not be accepted from an unidentified party without a report or an order from the public prosecution. Accepting the body under such circumstances, he said, amounted either to negligence or complicity on the part of those responsible for the morgue and hospital. He concluded that the death had resulted from torture, pointing out that the sheikh had been in good health before his detention and that his death within 48 hours of his abduction indicated that he had been subjected to severe torture. Saleh called on the authorities to identify those responsible and bring them to trial as quickly as possible. He said the incident had caused widespread fear, alarm, and anxiety among residents of North Kordofan because of the brutal and inhumane way in which the authorities had treated the victim. Condemnation The Kordofan Observatory also condemned the death of Ali Abdelrahman El Kajjam, who was detained by a security force at the livestock market in El Obeid on Saturday. His family received news on Sunday that his body had been found in the morgue of El Obeid Hospital, under circumstances that remain unclear. The observatory called for the immediate disclosure of the circumstances surrounding El Kajjam’s detention and the events leading to his death. It demanded a serious and independent investigation to establish the cause of death and hold accountable anyone found to have been involved in, or responsible for, violations against him while he was in custody. Monitoring and testimonies In a related development, the observatory said it had documented repeated cases of detentions involving civilians arriving from areas under RSF control. Some were reportedly detained at the entrances to El Obeid and subjected to interrogation and torture in an attempt to extract confessions that they belonged to the Rapid Support Forces. The observatory said it had received testimonies from three young men who reported being subjected to various forms of torture inside detention centres in El Obeid after arriving from areas of West Kordofan. According to their accounts, the abuses included beatings with whips and rifle butts, as well as threats to slaughter them, with knives held against their necks after they had been stripped of their clothes. The alleged torture was intended to force them to confess to belonging to the RSF. The young men said they were released after one of the security personnel recognised them and informed the force holding them that they had no connection with the RSF. The testimonies have raised concerns that civilians are being detained and tortured on the basis of suspicion or preconceived assumptions, without verification of their identities or evidence of involvement in military activities. Warning The Kordofan Observatory warned of the dangers of continued arbitrary detentions and torture in detention centres, amid the presence of multiple security forces and armed groups operating in the city and the absence of effective oversight and accountability. It said these practices placed the lives and safety of civilians at risk and opened the door to detentions based on suspicion or personal vendettas. The observatory stressed that geographical origin, or coming from areas under the control of one of the parties to the war, did not constitute evidence of military affiliation and could not justify depriving anyone of their freedom or subjecting them to torture or ill-treatment. It emphasised that the prohibition of torture and cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment is absolute under international law, and that such practices cannot be justified on grounds of suspicion or security requirements. Share article The post North Kordofan: Alarm as Sheikh detained in El Obeid found dead appeared first on Dabanga Radio TV Online .

items.title: Air Is Easing Out of the AI Bubble
items.description: Updated at 10:20 a.m. ET on November 23, 2026 This should be a bullish time for investors in the AI business. Nvidia, which designs most of the chips that have driven the AI boom, just reported that its sales and profits doubled year-over-year, and that it’s on pace to grow another 75 percent next year. The industry as a whole, Nvidia said, has a backlog of $2.5 trillion in future orders, meaning that demand remains strong. Anthropic, one of the industry’s two dominant developers of large language models, went public on Thursday and raised more money in its IPO than any company in history. Yet the dominant mood among investors is a sense of deep anxiety, not to say panic. Last Thursday, stocks soared when the market opened, buoyed by Anthropic’s debut. But by late morning, investors started selling, and by the end of the day the market was down more than 2 percent. On Friday, stocks sold off even more sharply, leaving the tech-heavy Nasdaq in negative territory for the year. AI companies are still collectively worth many trillions of dollars, but investors are looking at them, for the first time, with a more jaundiced eye. This is in part due to developments that few anticipated. The scandal at Nvidia , in which its founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, was forced to suddenly step down after revelations of multiple affairs, including one with a possible Chinese intelligence asset, has created turmoil at the company that has almost single-handedly propped up the entire AI industry. (The company unexpectedly reinstated him this morning, apparently thanks in part to President Trump’s advocacy on Huang’s behalf. Investors greeted the news by bidding up not just Nvidia's stock but tech stocks generally, which underscores the volatility of the market.) The Democrats’ massive victory in the midterms has also sparked doubt about the future of AI development. Many Democrats ran on a platform of slowing or even prohibiting the construction of AI data centers—an approach that resonated with voters, according to exit polls, and promises new political headwinds for the sector. [ Read: The scandal is bigger than Jensen Huang ] Even before Election Day and Huang’s unceremonious exit, a fundamental shift in the market’s attitude toward AI companies was under way. Since OpenAI released ChatGPT in 2022, investors have blithely poured money into the AI business on the assumption that somewhere down the road, it would become very profitable. Tech giants themselves have adopted the same strategy. Companies such as Google and Meta have spent hundreds of billions of dollars to build out their AI capabilities. But the sums of money required for this build-out are so immense—and the prospects for profit still so distant—that investors have, of late, become more demanding and less patient. At the moment, most of the money being spent on AI is being spent by AI companies, whether they’re constructing data centers or buying GPUs and memory chips from manufacturers or compute power from hyperscalers. There is a circularity to the business, whereby many of the companies in the industry are investing in and financing one another, while also selling to or buying from, or even competing with, one another. Earlier this year, Nvidia invested $30 billion in OpenAI, which in turn bought Nvidia chips. Anthropic, meanwhile, buys chips from Google, which is also one of its biggest investors—and one of its biggest rivals. There’s nothing wrong with this. When railroads were being built across the United States, much of the money came from companies in the rail industry. The same was true when the country electrified homes and industry. This is the nature of a massive build-out of infrastructure with anticipated future benefits. The key, though, is that in order for a build-out to be profitable—which is what investors care about—customers outside the industry will need to start spending huge sums on the product. This can take time; it took close to 30 years after the big commercial-rail build-out started for railroads to become sustainably profitable. In the case of AI, the sums necessary to turn a profit are truly huge. A number of recent studies estimate that AI revenues will have to exceed $3.5 trillion a year or more by 2032 just for companies to earn a 10 percent return on all the capital expenditures they’ve made so far. [ Read: The reluctant winner of the AI race ] If AI ends up radically reinventing entire industries, such as pharmaceuticals, these numbers are not impossible. But at the moment, it’s hard to see where all of that additional revenue would come from. Anthropic, for instance, has built a strong business licensing its LLMs; the company is currently on track to earn more than $80 billion in revenue over the next year. But Anthropic’s growth rate already appears to be slowing, even as the company is projected to spend at least $450 billion in capital expenditures over the next four years. Goldman Sachs recently estimated that Anthropic won’t generate free cash flow—meaning make more than it spends—until 2030. The challenge for AI companies is to convince businesses in the rest of the economy to start spending massively on AI, and soon. Right now, despite the hype surrounding AI, that is not happening. A recent study by Torsten Slok, the chief economist at Apollo Global Management, found that spending on AI was highly concentrated in a small number of firms. Companies don’t want to scrap existing investments in favor of AI until the business case for it is clear (and perhaps not even then). For many CEOs, the benefits of paying for the latest frontier model—as opposed to older models, or even open-source ones—remain uncertain. Slok’s study found no sign that AI has boosted productivity growth outside of big tech firms. AI could still transform the economy. But this shift may be more of a long, drawn-out process—similar, perhaps, to the way electrification transformed American industry in the early 20th century—rather than a fast and dramatic one. Investors, though, have bet that the transformation will be rapid, as have Big Tech companies themselves. If it turns out to be a marathon rather than a sprint, lots of AI stocks will have been seriously overvalued—which may help to explain why those stocks have been selling off in recent weeks. Apart from what it might mean for your 401(k), this is not a bad development. If AI is indeed a bubble, letting the air out slowly is much better than having it burst all at once. The market is signaling to companies that the cash spigot will not be open forever and that if they can’t find ways to monetize the hundreds of billions of dollars they’re already pouring into data centers and computing power, then they need to slow down. Given that AI companies themselves keep talking about the potential existential risks this technology poses, a slowdown might well be beneficial—socially, economically, and otherwise. Although these companies have implicitly promised investors that they will become the most profitable in history, the problem now facing AI firms is ultimately the one that haunts nearly any for-profit enterprise: At some point, and probably sooner than they may like, they will have to show investors the money.

items.title: Télécommunications : recalé au Conseil de l’UIT, le Gabon relativise son échec diplomatique
items.description: En lice pour intégrer le Conseil de l’Union internationale des télécommunications (UIT) sur la période 2027-2030, le Gabon n’a pas réussi à décrocher l’un des treize sièges réservés à l’Afrique. Malgré une campagne de deux mois et 77 soutiens revendiqués, Libreville entend capitaliser sur cette première tentative pour renforcer sa présence dans la diplomatie numérique internationale. Le ministre de l’Économie numérique, Mark-Alexandre Doumba, peu avant le vote, à Doha. © GabonReview/Capture d'écran Le rendez-vous de Doha n’aura finalement pas consacré les ambitions gabonaises. Le 16 novembre 2026, à l’occasion de la Conférence de plénipotentiaires de l’UIT (PP-26), les 194 États membres ont procédé à l’élection des 48 pays appelés à siéger au Conseil de l’organisation pour le mandat 2027-2030. Le Gabon ne figure pas parmi les élus africains, malgré les efforts diplomatiques déployés pour convaincre ses partenaires. Selon les résultats relayés par la presse nationale, le pays a terminé à la 18e place du scrutin africain, avec 77 voix, alors que 19 États se disputaient les treize sièges attribués au continent. Un revers pour la diplomatie numérique gabonaise, qui espérait accéder à cet organe chargé de piloter les orientations de l’Union entre deux conférences de plénipotentiaires. Un petit-déjeuner pour convaincre les délégations En marge des travaux à Doha, le ministre de l’Économie numérique, Mark-Alexandre Doumba, avait notamment organisé un petit-déjeuner en l’honneur des délégations participantes. En présence de la secrétaire générale de l’UIT, Doreen Bogdan-Martin, il avait présenté les ambitions numériques du Gabon et défendu sa candidature, sollicitant la confiance des États membres. La campagne, lancée en septembre à Nassau, aux Bahamas, avait mis en avant les priorités nationales en matière de connectivité, d'inclusion, de cybersécurité et de transformation numérique. Elle entendait également promouvoir la Déclaration de Libreville, issue de la Semaine du Numérique. Les 77 soutiens, un capital diplomatique à préserver Au lendemain du scrutin, le gouvernement a salué l’élection des treize représentants africains : Algérie, Côte d’Ivoire, Égypte, Ghana, Kenya, Maurice, Maroc, Nigeria, Rwanda, Sénégal, Afrique du Sud, Tanzanie et Tunisie. Le ministère de l’Économie numérique préfère retenir les acquis de cette campagne. En deux mois, le Gabon affirme avoir mobilisé « 77 soutiens de pays » , signe, selon lui, d’un intérêt pour sa candidature et d’un travail diplomatique à consolider. « Nous n'avons pas été élus cette fois-ci, mais nous restons membre actif de l'UIT » , souligne le ministère, qui entend poursuivre son engagement au sein de l’organisation. Et de conclure : « Nous reviendrons avec une expérience renforcée et une ambition intacte. Le chemin continue. » L’article Télécommunications : recalé au Conseil de l’UIT, le Gabon relativise son échec diplomatique est apparu en premier sur Gabonreview.com | Actualité du Gabon | .

items.title: Rencontres de Bamako : Quelle vitrine pour les photographes maliens ?
items.description: © Internet À quelques jours de l’ouverture des Rencontres de Bamako, la présence des artistes maliens dans la sélection officielle donne une visibilité particulière à la création locale. Reste à savoir comment cette exposition internationale peut se prolonger en reconnaissance professionnelle et rapprocher davantage la photographie de son public à Bamako. La 15 ème édition de la Biennale africaine de la photographie se tiendra du 26 novembre au 26 janvier autour du thème « Refabulation(s) ». Sur les 49 artistes retenus, 7 ont un lien déclaré avec le Mali, parmi lesquels Fatoumata Diabaté, John Kalapo, Aïssata Kané, Alfousseny Konaté et Oumou Traoré. La sélection résulte d’un appel international ouvert aux photographes et artistes visuels du continent et de la diaspora. Les propositions ont notamment été appréciées en fonction de leur relation avec le thème et de la démarche artistique développée. Pour les Maliens retenus, l’exposition offre une occasion de présenter leurs travaux devant des professionnels, commissaires, institutions et visiteurs venus de différents pays. John Kalapo, déjà présent lors de précédentes éditions, y voit un cadre important pour la scène photographique. « La Biennale africaine de la photographie joue un rôle essentiel dans la promotion de la créativité photographique, en soutenant la recherche, l’innovation et l’affirmation de nouvelles écritures visuelles », estime-t-il. Public La visibilité des artistes ne dépend toutefois pas uniquement du regard des professionnels étrangers. La fréquentation des expositions par le public malien constitue également une dimension importante de cette édition. Selon Tidiane Sangaré, Directeur général de la Maison africaine de la photographie, un programme de médiation doit mobiliser les écoles de formation artistique, les universités et les lycées. L’Institut national des Arts et le Conservatoire Balla Fasséké Kouyaté figurent parmi les établissements particulièrement ciblés. Le dispositif doit accompagner les visiteurs pendant les deux mois d’exposition. Une quinzaine de lieux privés sont également annoncés dans le programme « Off », en complément des principaux sites de la Biennale. Pour les photographes maliens, cette présence dans la programmation constitue une étape. La suite se joue aussi dans les rencontres professionnelles, les possibilités d’exposition après Bamako et la capacité à se construire un public local régulier autour de leurs œuvres. Ali Sankaré

items.title: Orwell Has Become What He Despised
items.description: “Orwell Saw This Coming” ran the headline, and if you didn’t read any further, you might agree. The president was whipping up hatred in elaborate rage-fueled rallies and plastering banners bearing his glowering, oversize face on government buildings. The National Guard was patrolling the streets of Washington. Officials in the recently renamed Department of War were bragging about extrajudicial killings. The national-security apparatus had divided the world into three zones of influence, strikingly similar to The Party’s Oceania, Eurasia, and Eastasia from 1984 . But none of that was the this in “Orwell Saw This Coming,” which ran in The Free Press in January. This was New York City’s new mayor. “It’s fair to say that George Orwell would have despised Zohran Mamdani,” the columnist Charles Lane argued. Trump was hardly mentioned. In 2026, if an American writer brings up Orwell, chances are high that their target is the left, not the right. Over the past decade, one of the strangest habits among right-wing intellectuals and pundits has been their use of Orwell to defend the rise of authoritarianism in the U.S. The reference is shockingly common . “If 1984 has a practical lesson, it is this: There is a world of difference between a despotism dedicated to the expansion of socialism through federal-government power and a despotism dedicated to dismantling it,” Nathan Schlueter wrote in 2017 in National Review . “The former suffocates; the latter, though not without its serious dangers, just might create room to breathe.” The most direct rebuttal to this absurdity is Orwell’s own: “My recent novel is NOT intended as an attack on Socialism or on the British Labour Party (of which I am a supporter),” he once wrote to a curious reader. Orwell was literally antifa. In Spain, he fought with the militia of the Workers’ Party of Marxist Unification. Barcelona has a square named after him, and not because he supported far-right authoritarians against academics and students, as many conservative intellectuals would seem to believe. [ From the May 2024 issue: What Orwell really feared ] Let’s call them the Orwellian Trumpists. They could not have misunderstood the writer, or the current political reality, any more thoroughly. To a certain extent, Orwell saw this coming. The dumbest mistakes are typically made by the intelligentsia, he once cautioned: “No ordinary man could be such a fool.” He has now become the subject of his own warning. Orwell transcends right and left in this sense: Everyone who writes a political opinion in English, whatever their persuasion, is following in his tradition. “Why I Write” and “Politics and the English Language” are the foundational texts of magazine and newspaper writing to this day. His style is so hard to replicate because it is so basic. Reading Orwell is like hearing a man say what he means. It’s an astonishingly difficult effect to imitate. I’m trying to write like him now. Almost every opinion writer you can name is trying to write like him too. The roots of right-wing Orwell worship are not hard to see when you consider his obsession with prose style and the debasement of political language. Orwell believed in political writing more than any other writer; he gave it a grandeur and a sense of purpose that play to the vanities of every opinion columnist. He believed in clarity, not just freedom of speech. Staleness, imprecision, and pretension were, for him, far more than technical flaws. They were signs of the onset of dehumanization. Over the past decade, as the banalities of identity politics entered academia and journalism, Orwell became an ideal lens by which to witness and critique the process. The left’s attempt to impose a new linguistic order by force of shame was, in fact, an attempt to repress the human. But the problem with today’s right-wing Orwellians is that they are living in the past. Trumpism is a far greater threat to the values Orwell fought for than wokeness ever could be. “The Orwellian Big Brother punishing you for expressing an impolitic thought is now the law of the land in the land of Orwell,” Rupa Subramanya, another writer for The Free Press , told a congressional committee last year. She said this while the Republican Party was detaining students for signing op-eds, and policing the border by looking for inappropriate social-media posts. DOGE, meanwhile, was pulling funding from government agencies on the basis of keyword searches. Everyone who has ever argued that the most significant threat to the Western canon comes from the left will need to reckon with the fact that Republicans were the ones who told professors to pull passages from Plato from a course at Texas A&M. It was Republicans who threw CDC data sets and significant chunks of the National Archives into a memory hole. Trump’s decrees about language have gone further than any Democrat ever dared: He changed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Lake Ontario, to his obedient followers, is Lake America. The Orwellian Trumpists’ claims to support linguistic freedom are laughable, or beside the point. In their bitter partisanship, they resemble the neoconservatives of a previous era, the liberals mugged by reality. They lack the dignity of their predecessors, though. They’ve been mugged by reality television. I think of them as the Otto intellectuals: Otto is the character from the 1980s British comedy A Fish Called Wanda who thinks that Aristotle was Belgian and that the central message of Buddhism is every man for himself. The contortions of the Orwellian Trumpists would dazzle any Soviet apparatchik. The British historian Niall Ferguson, who has used Orwell’s line that “to see what is in front of one’s nose needs a constant struggle” on multiple occasions, has frequently sane-washed Trump’s foreign policy. In an episode of the Hoover Institution’s podcast GoodFellows about Trump’s “coercive diplomacy,” Ferguson claimed that Trump’s destruction of America’s alliances and his sprawling, pointless violence were the result of deep strategic thinking. If you’re arguing in favor of “coercive diplomacy,” a phrase precisely as meaningful as “violent seduction,” you’re not George Orwell. You’re closer to Lord Haw-Haw. Sometimes, as with the right-wing activist Christopher Rufo, using Orwell has explicitly partisan purposes. “What happens is that the left will say, ‘Well you’re opposing DEI; you don’t like diversity, you don’t like equity, you don’t like inclusion,’” Rufo said on his YouTube channel. “And you can say no, those are false words, those are Orwellian terms.” Citing Orwell becomes a technique in such cases, although aimed at a negligible slice of the political sphere: people who have heard the word Orwellian but have never bothered to think through what it means. [ Thomas Chatterton Williams: The right is changing the rules of the culture war ] As Orwell wrote in “Politics and the English Language,” he hated any argument that “consists in gumming together long strips of words which have already been set in order by someone else, and making the results presentable by sheer humbug.” Orwell has become what he most despised. He has set the strips of words in order, and someone else is gumming them together by sheer humbug. He’s jargon now. He’s the jargon for the supposedly anti-jargon crowd. Orwell’s contradictory status reminds me of his magnificent essay on Charles Dickens. Orwell is as distant from us today as Dickens was from Orwell. He was trying to understand how Dickens could be appropriated by people he would obviously have despised. “Dickens attacked English institutions with a ferocity that has never since been approached,” Orwell wrote. “Yet he managed to do it without making himself hated, and, more than this, the very people he attacked have swallowed him so completely that he has become a national institution himself.” The audience remembered his sentimentality. The actual import of his writing vanished. Dickens was critical of virtually every entrenched system in English life but even more critical of the attempts to overturn those systems. Tradition was brutality; revolution was terror. Dickens walked a line between “attacking everybody and antagonizing nobody,” Orwell wrote. In the end, Orwell could not suppress his adulation for the contradiction, for the refusal to fit: Dickens was “a type hated with equal hatred by all the smelly little orthodoxies which are now contending for our souls,” he wrote. Those orthodoxies, unable to face Dickens’s recognition of their own fraudulence but unable to reject him because of the power of his writing, turned him into a vibe. The Dickens vibe remains in place today: squalid London, Christmas, cheekiness, wretched children. Orwell is being turned into a vibe just as Dickens before him. He is English to the fingertips: late-imperial, pre-multicultural, pubs with barmaids who call you “dearie,” memorized passages of Kipling, bad food, warm beer, and floggings in public schools—combined with a staunch criticism of every bit of that. Orwell was an Eton graduate who nonetheless described the upper classes as drunken, violent buffoons who were tolerable only at the moment they were being shot. At the same time, he was a committed leftist who became a critic of the totalitarian left as it took power across various states in the middle of the 20th century. The Orwell vibe is “aren’t English people clever?” meets “internal critic of the left.” As with Dickens, the vibe is half correct, half oblivious. The reason Orwell is such a paragon—the reason you can still feel the power of his writing long after every politician he mentioned is dead—is that he remained a party of one, even when he was shooting people or elephants, even when highly civilized human beings were flying overhead , trying to kill him. Now he exists through his contradictions: an Englishman who saw the brutality of England and yet remained English, a leftist who faced the brutality of communism and yet remained a leftist. “The words of a dead man are modified in the guts of the living,” as W. H. Auden said about Yeats. You can do what you like with Orwell’s words now. The Orwellian Trumpists have used their purported idol to justify a president who demands his followers accept obvious lies, who runs the government according to a standard of personal loyalty, who campaigns on two-minute hate, who revels in suspending the rules of war, who tears children from their mothers, who pardons for a fee, who has done everything in his power to separate language from meaning in order to camouflage his own brutality. They find themselves in an untenable position: Either they wanted all this or they have to admit that they got suckered by the most obvious con man in the history of con men. Perhaps it was inevitable that Orwell would devolve into just another vibe. But it’s shameful what that vibe turned out to be; the Orwellian Trumpists have chosen a boot stamping on a human face. It remains true that to see what’s in front of one’s nose requires a constant struggle.

items.title: The Big Reason Florida Is Still Red
items.description: When the midterms’ blue wave hit the southern United States a few weeks ago, one conspicuous red patch remained: Florida. There, unlike in nearby Georgia and Texas, Democrats running for senator and governor both lost their races—narrowly, but still. Much of the explanation for Florida’s enduring redness is that the state has absorbed hundreds of thousands of newcomers in recent years, and these individuals largely moved to Florida in order to be Republican . Starting in 2020, Florida became a magnet for Republicans from other states who yearned for a place with conservative politics and a relatively low cost of living. Research shows that people who moved to the state from around the country during the past six years were much more likely to register as Republicans than Democrats. And this month, many of these new arrivals voted to support the Republican policies that they’d relocated to enjoy. As the Republican senator Ashley Moody said in her victory speech on Election Night, many of the newcomers she met during her campaign “were desperate to hold on to what we have built here in this state.” For many years, Florida was a quintessential battleground. Liberal retirees largely settled on the state’s east coast, in solidly blue Miami-Dade, Broward, and Palm Beach Counties, while conservative retirees flocked to the panhandle and parts of the Gulf Coast. The state’s Democrats and Republicans largely balanced each other out: George W. Bush eked out a victory in 2000 in part by the grace of hanging chads , then won handily in 2004. Barack Obama won the state in 2008 and 2012; in 2016, Donald Trump beat Hillary Clinton by just over 100,000 votes. In 2018 , Democrats outnumbered Republicans in Florida by more than 200,000 registered voters. [ Read: Why people won’t stop moving to the Sun Belt ] Then came COVID. Many blue states had mask mandates, vaccine mandates, and prolonged school closures. Several of them placed new restrictions on policing after George Floyd’s murder or required the teaching of LGBTQ issues in public-school classrooms. Governor Ron DeSantis seized the opportunity to advertise Florida as a warm refuge from the cold winds of wokeness. He offered police officers a financial reward if they moved there from another state. He proclaimed the rise of the “free state of Florida”—even adding the line to highway welcome signs . “Occasionally you come across a tagline that really sticks, and that one did,” Susan MacManus, a political scientist at the University of South Florida, told me. The state’s lack of vaccine mandates, its aggressive school-reopening approach, and restrictions on teaching about sexual orientation were popular with right-leaning parents. So were the lack of state income tax and the prospect of going to the beach in February. A recent study by Daniel Smith, a political scientist at the University of Florida, and his colleagues found that, starting in 2020, the people who moved to Florida were much more likely to register on arrival as Republican than Democrat. Smith found that registered Republicans overall have lived in Florida a shorter amount of time than Democrats, and Democrats and independents from the Northeast are coming to Florida in much smaller numbers than they used to. By the beginning of this year, Florida had about 1.5 million more registered Republicans than Democrats. Republican candidates in Florida had other advantages in the midterms, too. Byron Donalds raised more than six times as much money for his gubernatorial campaign as his Democratic rival, David Jolly. And the state’s Hispanic population might have been especially receptive to attacks on Democrats. “Trump and then other Republicans really labeled the Democrats successfully as socialists,” Aubrey Jewett, a political scientist at the University of Central Florida, told me. That might have turned Cuban Floridians, many of whom had negative experiences with that country’s socialist government, away from any candidate even notionally associated with democratic socialism—such as Angie Nixon, Moody’s Democratic rival for the Senate. But experts I spoke with nevertheless said that migration from other states helped push Republicans over the top. Especially with remote work an option for large numbers of white-collar workers, Jewett said, “we have imported hundreds of thousands of Republicans over the last five years.” Paul Chabot, the CEO of GOP Agent, a real-estate company that connects people with conservative Realtors, told me that on top of good weather and a low cost of living, his clients “are looking at pro-gun-friendly states.” They don’t want to live in a state with “a George Soros–funded” district attorney, he added, “because they feel like they won’t be safe there.” So they come to Florida, where Governor-Elect Donalds has an A+ rating from the National Rifle Association and three-quarters of the state’s elected prosecutors are Republican. To understand the distinctiveness of this Republican influx, consider Florida alongside Texas, a historically red state that saw a blue wave in the midterms. Like Florida, Texas welcomed hundreds of thousands of migrants from other states from 2020 to 2026. But research has shown that newcomers to Texas were more evenly divided among Democrats, Republicans, and the unaffiliated, and have not affected the state’s partisan balance by much. The “majority of the people who are moving to Texas from other states are doing it for economic reasons or family reasons,” Mark P. Jones, a political scientist at Rice University, told me. [ Read: The simple message that produced a Democratic landslide ] Texas has seen some “political refugees” from California and other liberal states who do vote overwhelmingly Republican, Jones said. But left-leaning economic migrants seem to have arrived in larger numbers, and when many of them settled around Austin for tech jobs, they turned some of its surrounding counties blue, Jones said. In recent years, the state’s Republican politicians—three of whom had been in office for more than 10 years—were not popular, he added, and moderate Republican voters began to see Democrats as more palatable. Texas is still pink, Jones said—not quite purple. But, he said, “even a pink state can’t withstand an exceptionally unpopular president, a deeply flawed U.S. Senate candidate ,” and “a moribund economy that Republicans essentially hold all the responsibility for.” Whether Florida will continue on as a red state or shift back toward purple is unclear. Migration to the Sunshine State is slowing for a number of reasons. Some companies are calling remote workers back to the office, meaning that fewer people have the option to move wherever they wish. Plus, now that the COVID era is over, DeSantis is about to be out of office, and even some Democrats are disavowing the excesses of “ Woke 1 ,” the “free state of Florida” might not beckon the way it once did. Without a steady flow of conservative arrivals, the state could start tilting back to the center—or eventually to the left. People who were born in Florida are much less likely to be Republican than newcomers are, Smith said. And young voters, who are likelier to be Democrats, will eventually replace the state’s Baby Boomers as the latter go to that great beach house in the sky. Florida Democrats did notch some wins in the midterms: Pia Dandiya picked up a Florida House seat that “Republicans thought for sure they were going to win,” Smith said. Palm Beach County—home of Mar-a-Lago—went for both Jolly and Nixon in significant numbers. Many likely thought Texas was safely Republican too, until it wasn’t. Another definition of free , after all, is “up for grabs.”

items.title: We’ll Miss the Assistants When They’re Gone
items.description: T he executive assistants are being laid off. According to Bloomberg , firms such as PwC and McKinsey have cut thousands of assistant and other support-staff positions. From the start of 2023 until the summer of 2025, openings for entry-level jobs typically requiring at least some college dropped by 35 percent . What executive needs a 23-year-old with student loans and big dreams when they can use a personal AI assistant to manage their calendars and book their flights for free? You might think that this position is a perfect candidate for robot replacement. If AI can do mindless administrative tasks as well as any human, then all that’s left is the emotional labor, which can be heavy—managing the hyperspecific preferences and enormous egos of entitled corporate titans. Get rid of this position, and businesses would save money while young people would—perhaps—find less humiliating jobs. But I spent almost two years as an executive assistant, and one of the many things I learned was that no one—not even the bosses who might want to replace us—had any sense of what we actually did. These positions play an important role in the job market, providing a rare entry point into competitive fields. Executive assistants run last-minute errands. They steer their bosses away from annoying people at dinner parties and memorize faces and relationship histories. They know their boss’s intimate secrets and how to anticipate their needs. They put out fires before the boss smells smoke. They serve as office managers, nannies, baristas, and human encyclopedias. The better an assistant is at their job, in other words, the less anyone knows what they do all day. And when they’re gone, we’re really going to miss them. I f you ask executive assistants what they think about being replaced by AI, they might say that they welcome a robot taking over chores like filing expenses, but that they can’t imagine handing over the trickier parts of their job. Maguire Grace Amundsen was Kylie Jenner’s executive assistant for more than two years. She’s now a sort of girlboss influencer, and is starting an interview series with high-powered women called Hot Commodities . Being a good executive assistant, she told me, requires understanding “a lot that is not said.” You have to know “the person that you’re working for in a way where even if they don’t say something, you kind of know what they’re saying.” You have to understand their every mood. One woman, who used to be an executive assistant to a famous fashion designer and his chief marketing officer, and asked to remain anonymous because she had signed an NDA, said that if the designer “was in a good mood, it’s fine to send the email asking if it’s okay that the car is not a Range Rover for Friday. But if he’s in a terrible mood, sending that is literally going to kill your day.” “AI can’t predict all that,” she told me. Companies would need to “hire a human assistant to handle the AI assistant.” [ Sophie Gilbert: The Assistant and the messes women clean up ] Samantha, another former executive assistant, who asked me to use only her first name because she also signed an NDA, said that one of her most important roles was to serve as the scapegoat when anything went awry. She worked in the finance industry, and said a lot of her job was “taking the sword, and not taking that personally.” If something goes wrong anywhere in the company, you may be the one your boss yells at, and you get used to taking ownership for mistakes that weren’t your own. Samantha said she was privy to some of “the most intimate and personal things” in her bosses’ life: “colonoscopies, bonus sizes, who’s getting fired, who’s getting promoted, is divorce on the table.” The fashion assistant told me that the CMO’s “husband would call me. I talked to her driver. I talked to her hair stylist. I talked to her facialist. I talked to her kids. I talked to their school teachers.” At a time when most Americans distrust AI , it’s hard to imagine high-profile individuals wanting to share this kind of private information with a bot. But the more an executive assistant knows their boss, the more proactive they can be. High-powered executives often don’t have time to give instructions, and their assistants have to make judgment calls. “AI is really great at doing what you tell it to do, but a really good executive assistant is constantly thinking 345 steps ahead,” Samantha told me. “An EA needs to have the capacity to handle situations that don’t come with a clear set of instructions, whereas AI will always need a clear set of instructions.” Even if an executive theoretically fed an AI chatbot every bit of information (a big ask for someone who hires someone else to send their emails), there’s a level of nuance and emotional intelligence that you don’t get unless you are physically present in the room. Plus, most executives are looking to spend less time on their devices, not more. One of the main things assistants do is figure out what their boss actually needs to know from the onslaught of digital notifications and noise. “If you’re good at your job, you do a really great job of filtering, and I think that element would be lost,” Amundsen told me. To be fair, if you ask most anyone in most any field whether they think they can be replaced by AI, they’re likely to say absolutely not . But executive assistants have one more thing going for them: Perhaps the biggest reason executives like having them around is simply to flaunt them. “There is a level of prestige to having a dedicated assistant,” Anthony Taylor, an executive assistant at Hermès, told me. It’s how you know you’ve succeeded. He used to work at a smaller agency, where his old boss would bring him to events just to show that she was important enough to bring him to events. It’s the same reason that people send emails “looping my assistant in.” [ Annie Lowrey: How ChatGPT will destabilize white-collar work ] “No one’s going to be impressed by the fact that you’re paying some subsidiary of Claude to manage your calendar and your emails,” Taylor said. For this reason, human assistants will probably continue to have a place in status-obsessed industries that want to signal their refined taste, if nowhere else. These assistants don’t just book cars; they make sure the driver is wearing the right outfit and carrying the right brand of mints. They don’t just book the restaurant; they book the impossible restaurant, the kind you can’t get into unless someone at the hospitality group that owns the whole establishment owes you a favor. They cultivate their own network of maître d’s and publicists, and when their boss brings them to an event, they’re a status symbol in flesh and blood. T ake away the assistants , and lots of executives would probably have meltdowns. But that’s not what worries me most. The position of executive assistant is especially valuable for young people with backgrounds like mine. I would probably not be writing for this magazine if I hadn’t landed a job as an executive assistant here in 2023. I came from the South, had no connections in journalism, and little experience in the field. What I did have was a master’s degree, a résumé full of odd jobs, and the willingness to take notes in meetings. Eventually, I elbowed my way off the business side of the magazine and into writing. My story is a common one for people who want to land jobs in competitive, creative industries, but don’t have the perfect résumé or connections. “I was very unequipped, network-wise, moving to the city and pursuing fashion in any capacity, especially fashion PR, which is notoriously insular and elitist,” Taylor, who was raised in Mississippi, told me. When Taylor, who’s now 25, first set out to move to New York, he scoured the internet for anyone who could help him get his foot in the door. “My first actual successful attempt at networking was I strategically went on a date with someone who I knew worked in the industry,” he told me. It worked—his résumé was sent to a few agencies. He got an unpaid internship for a few months, during which he “spent all of my savings trying to stay afloat.” Eventually, a communications-assistant position that involved working on brand accounts opened up. He applied, but the role was given to the daughter of an executive at a major fashion magazine. The executive-assistant job was his “consolation prize,” he said. It required humility, but it was his ticket into the industry. Some people say that everyone should have to work a service-industry job, because there are certain life lessons that can only be learned as a 19-year-old bussing tables for snobby customers. My version of this argument is that everyone in corporate America should have to work as an assistant in their industry for a year. There are few jobs as frustrating and formative. You will learn to earn your keep. And if you’re as lucky as I was, you gain generous mentors who have successfully navigated the industry you want to be a part of. [ Matteo Wong & Charlie Warzel: AI agents are here. Nobody’s ready. ] You learn resilience: to take blame when no fault is your own, to humble yourself, to take menial tasks seriously, to go overlooked and unthanked. You learn to make judgment calls and not need external validation to know you’ve done a good job. But most of all, being an executive assistant makes you learn people , which is the most valuable skill in almost any industry. Young people need proof that there’s still a ladder left to climb in corporate America, and that if they’re willing to start on the lowest rung, swallow their pride, and be someone’s executive assistant, they can make it to the top. So, long live the human executive assistant. May their days be plenty and may their bosses be pleased with them. And if the bosses can’t be pleased, let them have the satisfaction of yelling at a 20-something, instead of a screen.

items.title: La Guinée s’inspire de l’expérience du PUDC sénégalais
items.description: Une délégation gouvernementale guinéenne a séjourné au Sénégal, du 16 au 21 novembre 2026, pour s'imprégner de l'expérience du Programme d'urgence de développement communautaire (PUDC), notamment en matière de financement, de réalisation d'infrastructures et de suivi-évaluation. Le modèle sénégalais du développement communautaire suscite l'intérêt de plusieurs pays africains. Dernière illustration : une délégation gouvernementale guinéenne, conduite par l'ambassadeur Kabélé Soumah, Secrétaire général du ministère du Plan et de la Coopération internationale, a effectué une mission d'échanges au Sénégal avec l'appui du Programme des Nations unies pour le développement (PNUD). Reçue le 17 novembre au siège du PUDC par son Coordonnateur national, Gade Kounta, la délégation a été édifiée sur le cadre institutionnel, les mécanismes de financement et les résultats du Programme. Celui-ci ambitionne de « faire en sorte qu'aucun Sénégalais ne soit laissé en marge du développement du fait de son lieu de résidence », a rappelé son coordonnateur. En un peu plus de dix ans, le PUDC a notamment réalisé plus de 1 090 kilomètres de pistes, électrifié plus de 1 170 villages, amélioré l'accès à l'eau potable dans plus de 2 050 villages et déployé plus de 5 800 équipements post-récolte. Des réalisations qui inspirent plusieurs pays africains, dont le Togo, la RDC, le Tchad, le Cameroun et la Gambie. Les 18 et 19 novembre, la délégation a effectué des visites de terrain dans les départements de Foundiougne et de Fatick. À Kébé Ansou et Keur Bakari Cissé, elle a découvert des infrastructures d'électrification bénéficiant à environ 1 765 habitants. À Sokone, une plateforme de transformation agroalimentaire traite jusqu'à 600 tonnes de noix de cajou au profit de 39 GIE. La mission a également permis de constater l'impact de la piste Passy-Thioyène, qui désenclave 36 villages et dessert plus de 22 000 habitants. À Ouyal Sandé, les visiteurs ont rencontré les 98 femmes du groupement Dialki Diék, qui assurent depuis 2019 la gestion de leurs équipements post-récolte. Grâce à leur organisation, elles ont constitué une épargne de 738 960 FCFA et acquis une broyeuse d'arachide sur fonds propres. La tournée s'est achevée au poste de santé de Ndiob, qui dessert 12 082 personnes dans 23 localités. La mission s'est poursuivie, le 20 novembre, au ministère des Finances et du Budget, autour des mécanismes de financement et du montage des projets, puis à l'Agence nationale de l'aménagement du territoire (ANAT). Au terme des échanges, plusieurs enseignements ont été retenus : le ciblage participatif des bénéficiaires, l'implication des communautés dans la gestion des ouvrages, la complémentarité des infrastructures et le rôle central de l'État dans la mobilisation des financements. Le Coordonnateur national du PUDC a toutefois insisté sur la nécessité d'adapter le modèle aux réalités de chaque pays, précisant que le programme « n'a pas vocation à être reproduit de manière uniforme ». Le Sénégal a ainsi réaffirmé sa disponibilité à accompagner la Guinée dans la conception et la mise en œuvre de son programme de développement local, en perspective notamment de ses ambitions dans le cadre de Simandou 2040.
